blocks.html: The horses had been gone four hours when Bayish Kenje uulu came down the river trail to Chong-Talas, and he knew it before he saw the corral.

He knew it from the dogs. The dogs of the stud farm barked at everything: at wolves, at the wind, at the director’s bicycle. Now they were silent, lying flat in the dust by the gate with their ears back, the way dogs lie when men have come in the night and struck them.
He knew it from the mare under him, too. The grey had lifted her head a mile back and smelled the empty air, and she had not liked it.
Bayish drew rein at the gate and sat a moment, looking.

The big corral was empty. Forty-one mares of the riding blood, the long-necked golden ones that the old men called akyel and the Red Army called “the Talas remounts”, and the black stallion Kara-Jal, who had cost the Soviet power two hundred gold roubles and a war. All gone. The herders had never liked the stallion. A black horse, the old men said, belonged to somebody else. The rails on the west side were down, cut clean with an axe, and the ground beyond them was trampled into a churned brown road that ran off toward the hills and the high cold country.

A man came out of the bunkhouse with a rifle he did not know how to hold. It was Pavlov, the director, a good engineer from Saratov, who had been sent to Turkestan to build a stud farm and had built one, and who had never in his life been asked to take it back from anybody.

“Kenje!” Pavlov said. It was what everybody called him. It meant the youngest son, though Bayish was thirty-four and had no brothers left alive. “Thank God. They came at two. Eight men, perhaps ten. They tied old Kalmurat in the hay barn. They shot Belka.” He pointed at a dog lying apart from the others. “I have telephoned Talas. The militia will come.”
“When?”
Pavlov looked at the ground. “Tomorrow. Perhaps the day after. They have one lorry and it is in Kara-Buura.”

Bayish nodded. He had expected that. He swung down off the grey and walked to the cut rails, leading her, and squatted there in the cold dust with his hat pushed back. He read the ground the way his grandfather had taught him, and then as the army had taught him again in the Fergana in ’21, when there had been men in the hills who would kill you for your boots.

A trail is a letter written by people who do not know you will read it. Bayish had heard an old ırchy sing that at a wedding once, and had thought it nonsense, and later in the Fergana had found that it was true.

This letter said a good deal. It said ten riders, as Pavlov had guessed, on mountain horses, unshod, the small round tracks of the Chongtor ponies that the herders rode. That meant men from the hills, men who knew the country. But among them one horse wore iron. A big horse, a cavalry horse, heavy on the forehand, and its near hind hoof turned out a little, so that it struck the ground crooked and left a track like a half-moon tipped on its side.

Bayish knew that track. He had followed it once before, four years ago, up a dry valley above Andijan, until the man riding the horse had turned in his saddle and shot the boy riding next to Bayish through the throat.

The man’s name had been Strelnikov. He had been a captain in the White army, then a captain of nobody, then a dealer in other men’s horses, and at the end of 1921 he had gone over the mountains into China, and everybody had said that was the last of him. Everybody had been wrong about him before.

Old Kalmurat was sitting on a feed box in the hay barn, rubbing the rope marks on his wrists. He was seventy, and had herded horses for the Kokand khans’ grandsons and for the Tsar’s remount officers and now for the Soviet power, and he regarded all three as passing weather.
“West,” he said, before Bayish could ask. “Up the Kenkol.”
“With forty mares heavy in foal? They’ll kill half of them on the pass.”

“They don’t care. They’re not selling foals. They’re selling horses.” Kalmurat spat. “Over the Kenkol, down the Chatkal, out to the Fergana. There are men in the Fergana still who’ll pay gold for a horse that can run all day. You know who.” He was quiet a moment. “There’s something else.” He did not look at Bayish when he said it. He looked at the barn door, where the light was coming in grey and thin. “Before they came. Around midnight. I went out to check the stallion, and there was a bull on the river path. A black one. Standing right in the middle of the path, looking at the corral.”
“Somebody’s bull got loose.”
“Nobody on this river keeps a black bull,” said Kalmurat. “Nobody would.”

Bayish said nothing. He had carried a Party card for six years and ridden with the Red cavalry for four, and he did not believe in Morkhan or omens or any of the things old men muttered about on the Talas. He had no more belief in them than in the idea that a horse would kick him if he walked behind it. He simply did not walk behind horses.
“I’m going after them,” he said.

Pavlov argued, as Bayish had known he would. It was madness. It was one man against ten. It was the job of the militia, of the OGPU, of somebody in Talas with a lorry and a telephone and a stamp. Bayish let him talk while he filled two water skins at the trough and packed the saddlebags. Flour. Salt. A twist of tea. Dried curd. A hundred and twenty rounds for the cavalry carbine he had brought home from the Fergana and was not supposed to have. A pinch of juniper in a scrap of white cloth, which his mother had put into every bag he had ever carried from home, and which he put in now without thinking about why.
“At least take a second horse,” Pavlov said, when he had run out of reasons.
Bayish turned to the grey mare. She stood quiet at the trough with her ears turned toward him, as she always stood, as if she had been listening all along and had already decided.

She was not a beautiful mare. She was too long in the back and too short in the neck, a Chongtor of no breeding, wall-eyed on the left side, so that strangers thought she was blind and she let them think it. Bayish had bought her from a Kökjal herder for a sack of flour and a pair of boots in the hungry spring of ’22, because she was the only horse in the market who had looked at him first. In three years she had never been lame, never been sick, never once refused a river.
“She’s enough,” he said.

He rode out of Chong-Talas at eight in the morning, with the sun just over the eastern ridges and the frost going off the stubble in long white breaths. He followed the churned road the stolen herd had made, west along the valley floor and then south into the mouth of the Kenkol, where the river comes down white and loud out of the mountains, between walls of red stone.
By noon he had found the first dead mare.

She lay in the river shallows where the trail crossed, a golden mare with a white blaze, her legs broken on the stones in the dark. They had not stopped to shoot her. Bayish got down and did it himself, though she was already nearly gone, and stood beside her for a moment afterwards with the carbine in his hands and the river noise all around him.
Then he got back up on the grey and rode on, faster.

All that afternoon the valley climbed. The juniper gave out, and then the birches, and then there was nothing but stone and the thin grass of the high pastures, already brown, and the wind coming down cold off the snow. The tracks went on ahead of him, up and up, and the crooked half-moon of the iron-shod horse was always among them, always a little apart from the rest, like a man who rides with a crowd and is not one of it.
At sunset he came round a shoulder of the mountain and saw the pass.

It stood at the head of the valley, a notch in the ridge against a sky going from gold to green to the colour of a knife, and below it the trail switched back and forth across a long slope of scree. Halfway up the scree, small as ants, he could see them. A string of horses. Riders. A dust of snow blowing off the ridge above them.
He was three hours behind. Perhaps less.
Then he looked up at the notch itself, and his hands tightened on the reins.
There was a rider on the pass.

He was alone, a little above the stolen herd, sitting a horse at the very top of the notch where the trail went over. The rider was only a shape against the green sky, and Bayish could not see his face. But the last of the sun was still on the pass, and it had found the horse, and the horse was white. Not grey, as Bayish’s mare was grey, but white, white as milk in a bowl, white as a felt laid out for a bride. And the rider sat there very still, with the whole cold sky behind him, and did not look down at the thieves below him on the scree, or at anything at all, except, Bayish was suddenly certain, at him.
The grey mare stood rock-still under him, her ears up toward the pass. That was what Bayish remembered afterwards: that his own hands were shaking on the reins, and the mare was not afraid at all.
He looked down at his hands. When he looked up again, the notch was empty.
Only the wind, blowing the snow off the ridge in a long white banner. Only the string of stolen horses, crawling up the scree into the dusk.

Bayish sat for a long while with the darkness coming up the valley behind him. Then he got down and made a small fire in the lee of a rock, the way a man makes a fire when he does not want it seen, and put a little of his mother’s juniper on it, and watched the smoke go straight up in the still air before the wind took it.
He was a Party man and a Red cavalryman, and he did not believe in any of it.
But he did not walk behind horses either.

[Translator’s note: the passage from “Then he looked up at the notch” to the end of the chapter does not appear in the 1964 edition. It is restored from the author’s typescript, in which a censor’s pencil has marked it “mysticism, cut”, and under that, in a different hand, “pity”.]
He slept two hours with his back against the rock and the carbine across his knees, and woke because the grey had moved.

She was standing over him in the dark with her head low, close enough that her breath was warm on his face. It was snowing. Not much, a thin dry snow that came down out of a sky he could no longer see and lay on the shoulders of his coat like flour on a baker. The fire was out. The juniper smell was gone. Somewhere up the valley a stone let go and went clattering down the scree for a long time, and then there was only the hiss of the snow.
Bayish got up slowly, because his legs were stiff with cold, and put his hand on the mare’s neck.
“All right,” he said. “I’m awake.”

It was perhaps three in the morning. The thieves would have made their camp on the far side of the pass, below the snowline, where there was grass and wood and shelter from the wind. They would not move again until light. A herd of forty mares heavy in foal does not cross a pass in the dark twice. If he went now, on foot, leading the grey, he could be at the notch before dawn and look down on them while they were still lighting their fires.

He did not think about the rider. He had decided that while he slept, without arguing. He had been tired. The light had been strange. There were herders in the Talas Alatau who rode white horses, and there was no law that said one of them could not be sitting on the Kenkol Pass at sunset, minding his own business, and then ride on down the other side.
He tightened the girth, checked the carbine, and started up.

The scree was the worst of it. In daylight it was only steep. In the dark, under an inch of new snow, it was a slope of loose stones that moved when you stepped on them, and every stone that moved took two others with it. The trail the herd had made switched back and forth across it, and he could follow it by feel more than sight, a band of trampled ground a little firmer than the rest, the snow lying differently on it, darker where the dung was.

He climbed with one hand on the grey’s mane and his head down. She came behind him without being asked, placing her feet in the places where his had been, the way a mountain horse will when she trusts the man in front of her, and twice when he slipped she stopped dead and let him catch hold of her and pull himself up.
Halfway up he found the second mare.

She had gone off the trail at a switchback and slid a little way down the scree and stopped against a boulder, and the snow had already begun to cover her. A chestnut, young, with a white sock on the near fore. Her neck was broken. There was a rope halter on her still, and the end of the rope had been cut. Whoever had been leading her had cut her loose when she fell rather than be pulled down after her, and had gone on.
Bayish crouched beside her for a moment in the dark. He brushed the snow off her face with his glove.
Thirty-nine, he thought.
Then he went on up.

The notch was a gap between two shoulders of black rock, wide enough for three horses abreast, with the wind coming through it so hard that the snow went sideways and he had to turn his face away to breathe. He stopped below it, in the lee of the eastern shoulder, and waited until the sky behind him began to turn the colour of ash.
Then he went up into the gap, slowly, with the carbine in his hands.
There was nobody there.

He had known there would be nobody there. He stood in the middle of the notch with the wind pulling at his coat and looked at the snow. It lay smooth and fresh across the whole of the gap, a hand deep, unmarked except by the herd’s trail, which came up out of the north side and went over and down the south. Forty horses and ten men had passed through here in the evening, before the snow, and their road was a wide grey trough with the new snow lying soft in it.
On either side of the trough the snow was perfect. No track of any horse, white or otherwise. Nothing had stood here since the snow began.
He walked the width of the gap twice to make sure. Then he stood still.

It meant nothing. The snow had come after. Whatever had stood here at sunset had stood here before the snow, and its tracks were under the snow with the herd’s, and there was nothing to see. That was all. A man who had read trails all his life knew that new snow lies about everything.
He did not walk the gap a third time.

The grey had come up behind him and was standing in the lee of the rock with her tail to the wind. She was not looking at anything in particular. He found that he had been watching her to see if she would.

The south side of the Kenkol drops away more gently than the north, in long benches of grass and stone, down into the head of a valley that runs south and west toward the Chatkal. The light was coming now, grey and flat, and he could see a long way. He went down a few hundred yards below the notch, to where a ridge of rock gave him cover, and lay on his belly in the snow and looked.

The herd was there. They had made their camp where he had guessed, on the first wide bench below the snowline, where a stream came down out of the rocks and there was a little thin birch for firewood. The mares were a dark patch on the white, close together for warmth, and beyond them were the horse lines and three fires with smoke going up straight in the still air of the valley, below the wind. He counted the fires twice. He counted the men in sight. Seven. Eight. Two more moving among the horses. Ten, perhaps, or nine.

And the big bay. He could pick it out even at that distance, standing apart on the horse lines, taller than the Chongtor ponies by a hand and more, with a blanket on it. Strelnikov had always looked after his horse.
Bayish lay in the snow and thought about it.

Ten men in a camp, with the light coming. One man on the ridge above them with a carbine and a hundred and twenty rounds. He could kill three, perhaps four, before they found cover. Then they would scatter into the rocks and the birches and work up the slope at him from three sides, and he would have no way down but the way he had come, and the scree at his back.
And the mares would run. Thirty-nine mares in foal, panicked by gunfire on a mountainside in snow. He would kill more of them than of the thieves.
He lay there long enough to be sure, and then he began to slide back down off the ridge.
That was when the shot came.

It came from below and to the right, from a tumble of boulders a hundred yards down the slope that he had looked at and dismissed, and it hit the rock six inches from his face and went away singing. Stone chips stung his cheek. He was already rolling, left, away from the ridge, down into a shallow gully that a stream had cut in summer, and the second shot came through the place where he had been.
Two rifles. He had heard them both. One heavy, an old Berdan perhaps, slow to load. The other lighter and quicker.

A rearguard. Of course there was a rearguard. Strelnikov had been a cavalry officer for twenty years before he was a thief. He had left two men in the rocks below the pass to watch the trail, and Bayish had walked up to the edge of the camp and lain down in plain sight of them like a recruit.
He lay in the gully with his face in the snow and cursed himself for a recruit.
The grey. Where was the grey?

He lifted his head an inch. She was still up by the ridge, in the lee of the rock, standing quite still with her ears pricked toward the boulders. She had not run. A shot went over his head, high, aimed at nothing, and she did not move.
Below, in the camp, men were shouting. He did not have long.

He looked at the gully. It ran down the slope at an angle, past the boulders where the riflemen were, perhaps forty yards to the left of them, and then on down toward the stream. It was not deep. A man on his belly would show his back.

He took his hat off, put it on the end of the carbine and pushed it up over the lip of the gully on the right. The heavy rifle fired at once and the hat jumped and spun away down the slope. He heard the man swear, and the clatter of the bolt, and he was already moving down the gully on his elbows and knees as fast as he could go, while the Berdan man reloaded and the other one looked at the place where the hat had been.

He got thirty yards before the second rifle found him. The bullet went into the snow by his knee. He came up on one knee in the bottom of the gully and fired three times at the boulders, fast, not aiming at anything, just to put stone in their faces, and went on.
Then he was below them, and to the side, and the boulders were between him and the camp.

He waited. He breathed. There they were, both of them, crouched in the rocks with their backs half to him, looking up at the ridge. One was a big man in a sheepskin with the old Berdan across his knees, thumbing a cartridge into it. The other was small and thin and had no hat.
“Put them down,” Bayish said.

The big man did not put it down. He came round with the Berdan, fast for a big man, and Bayish shot him through the body, and he sat down against the rock with a surprised look on his face and the rifle sliding off his knees into the snow.

The small one had turned too. He had his rifle half up. Bayish saw his face, and saw that it was a boy’s face, a boy of fifteen or sixteen with no hair on his lip and his mouth open, and he moved the carbine a hand’s width to the right and shot him through the upper arm.
The boy screamed and dropped the rifle and fell back against the boulder holding his arm.
Below in the camp they had stopped shouting. That was worse. There was the noise of horses, a lot of horses, and men calling to each other in low voices, and the scrape of saddles.

He went down into the boulders. The big man was dead, or would be. The boy was sitting in the snow with his back to a rock and his good hand clamped over his arm, blood coming out between his fingers, and he was crying without any sound, his mouth wide open, staring up at Bayish and waiting to be shot.

Bayish picked up both rifles and threw the Berdan down the slope into the snow. The boy’s rifle was an old single-shot Gras, French, from God knew what war. He worked the bolt. It was empty. The boy had fired his one cartridge and had not reloaded.
“Where are your horses?”
The boy pointed with his chin. Down, behind the boulders, two Chongtor ponies tied to a stunted birch.

Bayish looked down at the camp. They were not coming up. They were moving, and he knew why. The fires had been kicked out. Men were mounted and riding among the mares, getting them up, getting them moving, driving them down off the bench into the valley in a long dark stream, with the big bay at the head of it and a man on it in a long coat who turned once in the saddle and looked up at the pass.
He was too far away to see a face. But Bayish knew the set of the shoulders, and the way he sat a horse, as if the horse were a chair he had been born in.

Strelnikov was not going to waste a morning fighting one man on a mountainside. He had a herd to sell. He would leave the rearguard to their luck and be gone down the valley before the sun was high, and anyone who wanted the mares back would have to come down off the mountain after him into country he chose.

Bayish watched the herd go. He counted what he could. Thirty-nine, or near it. Kara-Jal was among them, black against the snow, his head up, fighting the rope. Bayish looked at the stallion longer than he meant to.
Then the boy made a sound behind him, and he turned round.

He went up for the grey. She had not moved from the lee of the rock. She stood there with the snow on her back and watched him come, and when he took her rein she pushed her nose once against his chest, hard, the way she did when he had been away too long, and he stood a moment with his hand on her face.
“I know,” he said. “I know. I was a fool.”

He brought her down to the boulders. The boy was still sitting where he had left him. He had stopped crying. He had got his belt off with one hand and was trying to tie it round his arm above the wound, and making a bad job of it, and his face had gone the colour of old snow.
Bayish knelt down beside him and took the belt out of his hand.
“Hold still.”

He cut the boy’s sleeve away with his knife. The bullet had gone through the meat of the upper arm, in at the front and out at the back, and missed the bone. Bayish had seen a great many worse. He packed the holes with snow to slow the bleeding, then with a pad torn from the boy’s own shirt, and bound it tight with the belt, and the boy bit on his lip and did not scream.
“What’s your name?”
The boy looked at him.
“I’m not going to shoot you,” Bayish said. “If I’d wanted to shoot you, you’d be sitting next to him.” He nodded at the big man. “Your name.”
“Nurdin,” the boy said.
“Nurdin who?”
“Nurdin Tölögön uulu. From the Chatkal.”
“Well, Nurdin Tölögön uulu from the Chatkal,” Bayish said, “your friends have left you.”
The boy said nothing. He looked down the valley where the dark stream of horses was going away into the morning, smaller and smaller, and his mouth moved, and then his face closed up like a door.
Bayish stood up. He considered the dead man in the sheepskin, and then the boy, and then the two ponies tied to the birch.
The sun came up over the eastern ridge while he stood there, and lit the whole south side of the Kenkol gold, and the snow on the pass above them blazed so bright that he could not look at it.
He did not look at it.
The ground was frozen too hard to dig, so they covered the big man with stones.

Bayish did most of it. The boy carried what he could one-handed, small flat stones from the scree, and laid them where Bayish showed him, and did not speak. When it was done there was a low grey mound against the boulders with the man’s boots sticking out of the end of it, because there had not been enough stones, and Bayish took off his own coat and laid it over the boots and then thought better of it and put it back on. A dead man does not need a coat. A live one does, on the Kenkol in October.
“What was he called?”
“Sapar,” the boy said. “He worked for the bai.”
“Which bai?”
The boy looked at him as if he were simple. “Abdyrakhman-bai. At Kök-Saz.”

Bayish nodded slowly. He had heard the name. Everyone south of the Talas Alatau had heard the name, the way everyone had heard of the weather. Abdyrakhman-bai owned flocks on six mountains and shops in three bazaars and the soviet of Kök-Saz, which had been elected in 1923 by a show of hands in the bai’s own courtyard, with the bai’s own men standing at the gate.
“Do you want to say anything?” he asked. “Over him.”

The boy hesitated. Then he took his hat off, which was not a hat but a strip of felt tied round his head, and stood at the head of the mound in the wind and said the short prayer that the Chatkal people say for the dead, the one that asks the White Rider to come down off the mountain for a soul and carry it home over the pass. He said it fast and badly, the way a boy says something he has heard old women say a hundred times and never said himself. At the end he said omin, and put the felt back on.

Bayish had not said that prayer since his mother’s funeral. He did not say it now. But he stood with his hat in his hand until the boy was finished, because it was not his business to stand any other way.

They went down the south side of the pass in the middle of the morning, leading the two ponies, Bayish on the grey. The herd’s trail was a brown road through the snow, easy to follow, and lower down, where the snow gave out, a brown road through the frost-burned grass, with the dung still steaming in places. They were an hour behind, perhaps two. Bayish did not hurry. He wanted to be an hour behind. An hour behind, he could read their trail. Ten minutes behind, they could read him.

The boy rode one of the ponies, holding the reins in his good hand, with the other arm strapped across his chest in what was left of his shirt. He was very pale. Twice he swayed in the saddle and Bayish thought he would fall, and twice he caught himself and sat up straight and looked ahead as if nothing had happened.

At noon they stopped by a stream and Bayish made him drink, and gave him dried curd, and looked at the arm. The bleeding had stopped. The skin round the holes was hot, but not too hot. Bayish had seen men lose arms from smaller wounds, and men keep them after worse. You could not tell, in the first days. You could only keep it clean and hope.
“Why did you do it?” he said.
The boy did not pretend not to understand. “For the rifle.”
“The Gras?”

“He said I could keep it. After.” The boy’s mouth twisted. “He said every man who rode with him got a rifle and a gold piece. Sapar said it was true. Sapar had two gold pieces. He showed me. They had an eagle on them.”
Tsarist coins. Bayish knew them. In 1919 half the Fergana had been paid in them, by one side or another, and the other half had been paid in paper that would not light a fire.
“Who said? Strelnikov?”
“The Captain.” The boy said it in Russian. Kapitan. “Everybody calls him that. The bai calls him that.”
“How long has he been at Kök-Saz?”

“Since the summer. He came over from the Fergana in the summer with six men and some horses. He stayed at the bai’s. He bought horses, and he sold horses, and he paid in gold.” The boy looked at the stream. “Then in the autumn he said there would be a big job. Over the Kenkol. He needed men who could ride and men who knew the passes. I know the passes. My father took the sheep over the Kenkol every year before...” He stopped.
“Before what?”
“Before he died.”

Bayish did not ask how. There were only two ways a man from the Chatkal died, in the years when this boy was small. In 1916 they had gone over the passes into China, the whole valley, with the Russian soldiers behind them, and half of them had died on the ice. And in the years after, the ones who came back had died of what they brought back with them.
“The herd,” he said instead. “Where does it go?”

“To Kök-Saz. To the bai’s. They’ll rest them two days in the bai’s yard, and then they go south.” The boy pointed with his chin, down the valley and beyond it, to the far brown hills in the haze. “Over the hills, to the Fergana side. There’s a man there who will buy them. The Captain says he pays better than anybody.”
“Which man?”
The boy looked at the ground. “I don’t know his name. They call him the Kurbashi. The Black Kurbashi.”
Bayish knew that name too.

He sat by the stream with his elbows on his knees and looked at the water going over the stones, and for a while he was not in the Chatkal at all. He was in a dry valley above Andijan, in the summer of 1921, with the sun so hot that the rocks burned your hands, riding at the head of a patrol of nine men with a boy beside him called Ilyas.

Ilyas had been seventeen. He had lied about it and said nineteen, and nobody had believed him, and nobody had cared. He came from the upper Talas, from a village near Bayish’s own, and he had attached himself to Bayish on the first day the way a foal attaches itself to a horse that is not its mother, and Bayish had let him, because it was easier than not. Ilyas talked. He talked about horses and girls and the city of Tashkent, which he had never seen, and about what he was going to do after the war, which was to breed horses, a whole herd of them, golden ones, on the upper Talas, and sell them to the army for a fortune.

They had been following a band of horse thieves who were selling to the basmachi. The thieves had a White officer with them, everybody said, a Russian, who rode a big bay with a crooked hind foot. They followed the half-moon track for two days up the dry valley. On the third day the man on the bay turned in his saddle at four hundred yards, at a gallop, with the sun behind him, and fired once with a cavalry carbine, and Ilyas went off his horse backwards and lay in the dust with his throat open and his hands moving.

It had taken him a quarter of an hour to die. Bayish had held him the whole time. He had talked to him, though he could not remember afterwards what he had said. He thought it might have been about the golden horses.
The Black Kurbashi had been the basmachi commander in those hills that summer. He had been buying.
“You know him,” the boy said. “The Captain.”
Bayish looked up. The boy was watching him with his pale face and his dark eyes, and Bayish saw that he had been watching for some time.
“I know his horse,” he said.
He stood up and went to the boy’s pony and took the Gras rifle out of the saddle boot where he had put it that morning. He worked the bolt, to show it was empty, and held it out butt first.
The boy stared at it.
“Take it,” Bayish said. “It’s yours. You earned it. You stood your watch and fired your round. That’s more than most of them do.”
The boy took the rifle slowly with his good hand. He held it across his knees.
“There’s no cartridges,” he said.
“No,” Bayish agreed. “There’s no cartridges.”
He pointed west, down the stream, where it went away from the herd’s trail toward a side valley and a long brown slope with sheepfolds on it, small grey squares of stone, and smoke.
“Is that the way to your mother’s?”
The boy said nothing for a moment. Then he nodded.

“Go home,” Bayish said. “Tell her you fell off a horse. Tell her whatever you like. Keep the arm clean. Wash it in salt water, if she has salt. If it goes black, go to the doctor in Talas, not to a bakshy.” He gathered up the grey’s reins. “And stay off the Kenkol.”
He swung up into the saddle. He took the rope of the second pony, the dead man’s, and turned the grey’s head down the valley, onto the herd’s road, and rode away without looking back.
He had gone perhaps a mile when he heard the pony behind him.

He did not turn round. He rode on at the same pace, along the brown trail through the burned grass, with the dead man’s pony on its rope behind him and the river loud on his right. After a while the sound of the second pony came up a little closer, and then stayed there, fifty yards back, matching his pace.
At the next stream crossing he stopped to let the grey drink, and sat in the saddle looking at the water.
The boy stopped too, fifty yards back, and sat on his pony with the empty rifle across his knees and his strapped arm against his chest, and looked at the water as well.
Neither of them said anything for some time.
“Your mother,” Bayish said at last, not loud, so that the boy had to come a little closer to hear, “is going to be very angry with you.”
“Yes,” the boy said.
“And with me.”
The boy thought about that. “Yes,” he said. “Probably more with you.”

Bayish looked away down the valley, where the herd’s trail went on and on into the haze, toward Kök-Saz and the bai and the Captain and the hills beyond, and further than that, the Fergana, and the Black Kurbashi, and a dry valley above Andijan where a boy of seventeen had lain in the dust with his hands moving.
He was not going to have another one. He knew that much. He would send this one home tonight, if he had to tie him to the pony and lead him there himself.
“You know the passes,” he said.
“Yes.”
“You know Kök-Saz. You know the bai’s house. The way in and the way out.”
“Yes.”
Bayish nodded. He picked up the grey’s reins.
“Ride beside me, then,” he said. “Not behind. A man who rides behind me, I shoot.”
The boy brought his pony up level, carefully, on the grey’s off side, and they went on down the valley together, and neither of them said any more about the boy’s mother for the rest of that day.

They camped that night in a stand of birch above the river, without a fire. The boy slept at once, with the rifle in his good arm like a child with a doll. Bayish sat up with his back against a tree and the carbine across his knees and watched the dark.

Toward midnight the boy began to talk in his sleep. Fever talk, quick and low, in the Chatkal dialect with its old church words. Bayish could not follow most of it. Once, quite clearly, the boy said “Ene”, mother, and once he said a name that might have been his father’s.
Bayish got up and found the boy’s forehead with his hand. It was hot, but not burning. He wet his own scarf in the river and laid it across the boy’s face, and sat down again.

Below them in the dark, very far off down the valley, a horse called. One long rising whinny that went on and on and broke at the top, the way a stallion calls when he is penned among strange horses and does not like it.
Kara-Jal, Bayish thought. He was certain of it, though he could not have said why.
He sat and listened until the sound stopped. Then he sat and listened to the silence, and the river, and the boy’s breathing, until the sky in the east began to grey.

Aimkan’s winter camp was three stone houses and a sheepfold on a shelf of the side valley, with a stream below and a stand of poplars that had dropped their leaves, so that the yellow lay thick on the ground and the bare white trunks stood up out of it like candles. There was smoke from one of the houses. A dog came out to meet them, barking, and then stopped barking and ran back again, and a woman came out of the door with a ladle in her hand.

She stood in the doorway and looked at her son on the pony, with his arm strapped across his chest and his face the colour of whey, and at the stranger on the grey mare beside him, and at the empty rifle. She did not say anything.
Then she put the ladle down on the step, very carefully, the way you put down something you might otherwise throw.
“Get off that horse,” she said to her son.
Nurdin got off. He did it badly, one-handed, and nearly fell, and his mother did not move to help him. He stood in front of her in the yellow leaves with the rifle in his good hand.
She hit him once, open-handed, across the face. Not hard.
Then she took his face in both her hands and held it, and looked at it, and did not let go.
Bayish sat on the grey and looked at the poplars.

Her name was Aimkan, and she was perhaps forty, though the mountains had made her look older. She was tall and straight, with a long face and dark eyes like her son’s, and she wore the white elechek of a married woman, wound high and tight, though her husband had been dead for eight years. She brought Bayish into the house because he was a guest and there was no other way to treat a guest, and she sat him on the felt in the place of honour, and she brought him milk and bread and a bowl of mutton broth, and she did not once look at him while she did it.
When Nurdin told her who had shot him she was silent for a while, holding the teapot.
“You,” she said to Bayish.
“Yes.”
“You could have killed him.”
“Yes.”
She poured his tea. Her hand was quite steady. “Why didn’t you?”

Bayish thought about lying, and did not. “I had a boy beside me once,” he said. “In the Fergana. About his age. A man with a carbine killed him.” He drank some of the tea. It was very strong, with salt and milk in it, the way they make it in the Chatkal. “It’s the same man your son was riding for.”
Aimkan put the teapot down.

She looked at her son, who was sitting by the stove with a bowl of broth he had not touched, and then at Bayish, and then at the window, where the light came in grey through a pane of thin scraped hide.

“My husband,” she said, “was called Tölögön. In the summer of the Great Flight, when the soldiers came up the valley, he took us over the Kenkol and the Suusamyr and the Kökjal passes into China. Me and this one and his sister. On the ice above the Kökjal his sister died, and he carried her two days before he would let me put her down. In China he worked for a Chinese merchant for nothing, for a bowl of rice a day, and in the spring of the next year we came back over the same passes, and on the Kenkol he fell in the snow and did not get up.” She said it quite flatly. “So my son knows the passes. His father showed him every one of them.”
Bayish said nothing. There was nothing to say. Half the families in the Talas and the Chatkal had a story like it.

“And when we came back,” Aimkan said, “there was nothing. The houses were burned. The sheep were gone. The Russians had the bottom land. And Abdyrakhman-bai, who had not gone anywhere, who had sat in his house at Kök-Saz all through the troubles selling bread to the soldiers, he lent us sheep. Forty sheep, to start again.” Her mouth went thin. “That was eight years ago. I have paid him back two hundred.”
“And you still owe him.”

“I still owe him forty. Every year I still owe him forty. That is how a bai lends.” She looked at her son. “So when the Captain came and said there was a rifle and a gold piece for a boy who knew the passes, and the bai’s man Sapar said the bai would forgive the debt if he went, what was a boy of sixteen going to do?”
Nurdin was staring into his bowl. His ears had gone red.
“He was going to do something stupid,” Aimkan said. “Like his father.”

After the meal she sent the boy to lie down in the other room, and he went without arguing, which told Bayish how bad the arm was. Aimkan unwound the bandage herself and looked at the wound and said nothing, and washed it with salt water that made the boy go white and silent, and bound it up again with clean cloth. When she came back she sat down across the stove from Bayish and folded her hands.
“Now,” she said. “What are you?”
“I break horses at Chong-Talas. The state stud.”

“No. What are you?” She pointed with her chin at the carbine, which was leaning against the wall by the door, and then at his coat, where the Party card was, though she could not have known that. “You talk like a soldier. You shoot like a soldier. You go after ten men alone like a fool. Are you the OGPU?”
“No.”
“The militia?”
“No.”
“Then what?”
Bayish turned his bowl in his hands. “I’m the man who looks after the horses,” he said. “Somebody took the horses. So I’ve come to get them back.”
Aimkan looked at him. Then she laughed, once, without any pleasure in it.

“You are a fool,” she said. “Listen to me. You don’t know what you’re riding into. Abdyrakhman-bai is not a thief. He is the soviet. He is the law in this valley. When the commissars came in ’23 and said there must be a soviet in Kök-Saz, he called a meeting in his courtyard, and his men stood at the gate, and everybody put up their hands, and now he is the chairman. He has a stamp. He has a paper from Tashkent with a seal on it. If you go into Kök-Saz with that rifle and say he has stolen state horses, he will have you arrested as a bandit by his own soviet, and sent to Tashkent with a letter, and you will never see the Talas again.”
“I’m a Party member.”
“So is he,” said Aimkan.
Bayish put his bowl down.

He had not thought of that. He should have. In 1923 every bai in Turkestan who could read had joined something, the Party or the Koshchi union or the soviet, the way a man puts on a coat when the weather changes. He had seen it in the Fergana. A man who had paid the basmachi in the morning would be at a Party meeting by the afternoon, making speeches about the class enemy.

“And the Captain,” Aimkan said. “The Captain is the bai’s guest. You understand? Under his roof, at his table. If you touch the Captain in the bai’s house, you insult the bai, and every man in the valley who owes him sheep will be on the bai’s side. And every man in the valley owes him sheep.”
They sat in silence for a while. Outside, the wind had got up and was moving in the poplars, and the yellow leaves went past the window in a slant.
“Tell me about his house,” Bayish said.
Aimkan looked at him. “You’re still going.”
“Tell me about his house.”

She told him. She told it well. She had walked past it every week of her life and hated it every time. The bai’s compound stood at the top of the village of Kök-Saz, where the valley widened and the river ran slow among reed beds. A mud-brick wall twice the height of a man, with a wooden gate on the village side, and the bai’s houses inside, and storerooms, and a big yard with a well and a mulberry tree. Behind the houses, against the hill, a second yard, with stables along the back wall. That was where he kept his horses. That was where the mares would be.
“Is there another way in? Besides the gate?”
Aimkan hesitated. Then she said: “The aryk.”

The irrigation channel, she said, came off the river above the village and ran down along the foot of the hill, and the bai, who had paid for it to be dug and who took more of its water than anyone, had had it brought in under the back wall of his compound to water the stable yard and the mulberry and his wife’s flowers. There was a hole in the bottom of the wall where it went in, with a grating of wooden bars across it. Children went in and out under the grating in summer when the water was low, to steal mulberries. In autumn the water was low.
“How low?”
“To the knee. Lower, now.”
“How do you know?”
Aimkan looked at the door of the other room, where her son was lying.
“Because he was one of the children,” she said.

Bayish slept that night on the felt by the stove, with the carbine beside him, and woke before dawn to find Aimkan already up, kneeling by the fire, blowing it into life. Nurdin was standing in the doorway of the other room, fully dressed, with his strapped arm and the empty rifle.
Aimkan did not look round.
“You can’t come,” Bayish said to the boy.
“I know the aryk.”
“Your mother knows the aryk. She’s told me.”

“She doesn’t know where the grating’s loose.” The boy’s chin came up. “I do. And I know which dog is which. And I know the bai’s stableman, Kudaibergen, who drinks. And I know the bai’s son, who is a coward, and which room he sleeps in. You don’t know any of that.”
“No,” Bayish said. “I don’t.”
He looked at Aimkan. She was still blowing on the fire, very carefully, and did not look at either of them.
“If he comes,” she said, without turning round, “and he dies, you owe me kun. A man’s blood-price, for my son. Before the elders. Ninefold.”
“I don’t have it.”
“No,” Aimkan said. “Nobody does.” She sat back on her heels and looked at the fire, which had caught now, the flames going up yellow round the dung cakes. “So you had better not let him die.”

She got up. She went to the chest by the wall and opened it and took out a strip of white felt, a long narrow strip of the kind that is tied to a cradle or a saddle or the branch of a holy tree, and came over to the door, past her son, and out into the grey morning where the horses were. Bayish followed her. She went to the grey mare, who stood quiet and let her, and she tied the strip of white felt to the brow band of the mare’s bridle, between the ears, with a knot that would not come undone.
“So that he knows her,” Aimkan said.
“Who?”
She looked at him as if he were simple, the way her son had looked at him on the mountain.
“The one who comes down off the pass for souls,” she said. “So that if he comes for one of you, he knows which horse to bring back.”
Bayish looked at the white felt on the mare’s brow. He had a Party card in his coat, and a carbine, and a hundred and fifteen rounds.
He did not take the felt off.
He rode into Kök-Saz at noon, alone, by the main road, with the carbine in its boot under his leg and his hat on straight, like a man who had business and nothing to hide.

He had left the boy in a ruined sheepfold on the hill above the village, with the two ponies and the empty rifle and strict instructions, and the boy had looked at him with his dark eyes and said yes to all of them, and Bayish had not believed a word of it. But there was nothing to be done about that. You cannot tie a boy of sixteen to a sheepfold.

Kök-Saz lay where Aimkan had said, where the valley opened out and the river went slow and brown among the reed beds that gave the place its name. Forty houses, perhaps fifty, flat-roofed, mud-brick, with poplars round them and the stubble of the harvest on the terraces above. A mill. A shop with a tin sign in Russian and Arabic letters. A small square of beaten earth with a mulberry tree in it and three old men sitting under the tree on a felt, who watched him ride past and did not stop talking.
And at the top of the village, against the hill, a wall.

It was as she had said. Twice the height of a man, mud-brick on a stone footing, whitewashed once and long ago, with the wash coming off in patches like old skin. A big double gate of poplar wood, studded with iron. Over the gate, nailed to the wood, a board with red letters on it in Russian and in the old Arabic letters that Iradi was still written in then, which said that this was the Soviet of Workers’ and Peasants’ Deputies of the Kök-Saz Village Council.
The gate was open. Bayish rode through it.

The bai received him on a raised platform under the mulberry tree in the inner yard, on a heap of carpets and cushions, with a samovar going at his elbow and a boy to pour. He was a heavy man of fifty or so, with a grey beard trimmed close and small clever eyes in a soft face, and he wore a quilted silk coat over a Russian shirt with a collar, and a Party badge on the coat. He did not get up.
“A guest,” he said, and smiled. “Sit. Sit. Tea. You have come over the mountain? In this weather? Sit.”

Bayish sat on the edge of the platform. He took the bowl of tea the boy gave him. He looked past the bai, across the yard, to the second gate in the far wall, where the stable yard would be. It was shut. Behind it, quite clearly, came the sound of horses. A lot of horses. And once, high and angry, a stallion calling.
“You have fine horses,” he said.
“Horses?” The bai spread his hands. “A few. I am a poor man. I keep a few horses for my sons.” He sipped his tea. “You are from the Talas, by your voice.”
“From Chong-Talas.”

The bai’s face did not change at all. Bayish gave him that. “Ah,” he said. “The state farm. The Russian’s farm. The horses for the Red Army. A great work. A great work of the Soviet power.” He set his bowl down. “And what brings a man from the state farm so far over the mountain?”
“Forty-one mares,” Bayish said. “And a black stallion. Stolen four nights ago. Their trail comes into your yard.”
There was a silence under the mulberry tree. The boy who poured the tea had stopped pouring.
Then the bai laughed, the comfortable laugh of a fat man at a joke he has heard before.

“Stolen?” he said. “My dear friend. Nobody has stolen anything. I bought them. Last week. In good faith, from a dealer, with a paper.” He clapped his hands, and a man came out of the house, a thin man with spectacles, and the bai said something to him, and the man went back in. “You’ll see. A paper with a stamp. From your own director. The Russian. He sold them because the state has no money to feed them over the winter. Everybody knows the state has no money. You’ll see.”
The thin man came back with a paper. The bai handed it to Bayish with a little bow, as if it were a gift.

Bayish read it. It was in Russian, typed on a good machine, and it said that the Chong-Talas State Stud, by order of its director, had sold to the citizen A. Abdyrakhmanov of Kök-Saz forty-two horses of the riding type, surplus to requirements, for the sum of four thousand roubles in chervontsy, paid in full. It was signed Pavlov. There was a round purple stamp.
It was a very good paper. It was so good that for a moment, holding it, Bayish was not sure.

Then he looked at the signature again, and was sure. Pavlov signed his name with a great sweeping tail on the final letter, like a man signing for a whole railway. This one had no tail. Whoever had forged it had seen Pavlov’s name typed, but never written.
“It’s a fine paper,” he said, and handed it back.

“You see?” said the bai happily. “A misunderstanding. Your director has forgotten. Directors are always forgetting. You will go home and tell him, and he will remember, and he will be very ashamed, and we will all laugh about it.” He leaned forward a little on his cushions, and his small eyes were not laughing at all. “And if he does not remember, well. There is the soviet. There is the law. I am the soviet, here. You understand me? Here, I am the law.”
“He doesn’t understand you, Abdyrakhman,” said a voice behind Bayish, in Russian. “He’s a soldier. Soldiers never understand anything. That’s why they make such good soldiers.”
Bayish turned round.

The man standing in the doorway of the house was tall and thin and perhaps fifty, with a long tired face and a short beard gone grey at the corners of the mouth. He wore a good English coat that had been very good once and was now only good, and riding boots that had been mended by someone who knew boots. He had a glass of tea in his hand, in a silver holder, the Russian way. He looked at Bayish with an expression of mild and courteous interest, like a man meeting someone at a railway station whom he has been told to expect.
“Captain Strelnikov,” the bai said, with a wave of his hand. “My guest. A dealer in horses. A very honest man.”

“Thank you, Abdyrakhman,” said Strelnikov. He came across the yard and sat down on the edge of the platform, a little way from Bayish, and crossed his legs, and drank his tea. “And you,” he said to Bayish, pleasantly, in Iradi now, a good careful Iradi with a Russian edge to it, “are the man who killed Sapar on the Kenkol. And shot a child. The rearguard told me. The one who came back.”
Bayish said nothing. There had been no one who came back. The man was guessing, and guessing well.

“You came up the scree in the dark,” said Strelnikov. “Alone. On a Chongtor mare. And lay down on the ridge in full view of my picket like a cadet on his first exercise.” He shook his head. “I nearly had the camp turned out for you. Then I thought, no. Let him come. A man who comes that far alone is either a fool or a man with a reason. And I wanted to see which.”
“Which am I?”
Strelnikov considered him over the rim of the glass.

“Andijan,” he said. “Wasn’t it? The summer of ’21. The dry valley. You were the scout. You were always out in front. You rode a bay with a white face, and there was a boy with you who never stopped talking.” He set the glass down on the carpet. “I’m sorry about the boy. I was aiming at you.”
Bayish sat very still. The tea bowl was in his hand. He found that he had to think about not crushing it.
Across the yard, behind the shut gate, the stallion called again.

“I’ll make you an offer,” Strelnikov said, and now he was not smiling. “Because I liked the way you came up the scree, and because I’m tired, and because I have shot enough of you people for one lifetime. Twenty gold pieces.” He took a small leather bag out of his coat and set it on the carpet between them. It clinked. “Tsarist. With the eagle. Enough to buy a house in Talas and a wife to put in it. You go home. You tell your Russian the mares were dead on the Kenkol, or sold, or flown away to heaven. Nobody will ever know. In a month I will be in Kashgar, and Abdyrakhman will be a richer man, and your Soviet power will buy forty more mares from somebody else and never miss these.”
“And if I don’t?”
Strelnikov sighed. He stood up, and brushed his coat, and picked up his glass.

“Then sometime in the next few days,” he said, “somebody will shoot you. Probably me. And I’ll be sorry about that, too.” He looked down at Bayish. “Think about it. Abdyrakhman will give you a bed for the night. He’s very hospitable. You’ll be quite safe under his roof. Won’t he, Abdyrakhman?”
“Quite safe,” said the bai. “A guest is sacred.”
Strelnikov nodded, and went back into the house.

Bayish sat a moment longer. He put down his tea bowl, untouched, and left the bag of gold where it lay. He stood up and bowed to the bai, the short bow of a guest leaving, and walked back across the yard to where the grey was tied, and untied her, and mounted.
“You will not stay?” said the bai, surprised.
“I have to see a man about some sheep,” Bayish said, and rode out of the gate.

He went back up the hill to the ruined sheepfold, by a long way round, watching his back trail. The boy was not in the sheepfold. The boy was flat on his belly on a rock above it, where he could see the whole of the village and the bai’s compound, with the empty Gras beside him, exactly where he had been told not to be.
“I said stay in the fold.”
“You’d have done the same,” said Nurdin.
Bayish thought about it. “Yes,” he said, and lay down on the rock beside him.

From up there you could see into the bai’s back yard, over the wall. The mares were there. Bayish counted them, slowly, twice. Thirty-nine. Packed into the stable yard, which was not big enough for half that number, standing nose to tail in the mud, with hay thrown down on them from the stable roof. In one corner, on his own, roped to an iron ring in the wall, the black stallion, who would not stand still, who kept swinging his quarters and throwing his head against the rope and squealing, so that the mares nearest him pressed away.
“Tonight,” Bayish said.
They went in at two in the morning, by the aryk.

The water was colder than Bayish had believed water could be, and came above the knee, and the bottom was soft mud that pulled at his boots. They went along the foot of the wall in the dark, with the water talking softly round their legs and the stars very bright and cold overhead, and came to the place where the channel went under the wall into a low black arch, with the grating across it.
The boy put his good hand on the third bar from the left and pulled, and it came out of its socket in the mud as easily as a tooth from an old man’s jaw.

They went through on their bellies in the water, one after the other, Bayish holding the carbine above his head. On the other side was the stable yard. It stank of horses and wet hay and dung. The mares were dark shapes standing close together, breathing, shifting, and the smell of strangers went through them like wind through grass. Bayish stood in the mud with the water running off him and spoke to them, low, in the voice he used at Chong-Talas in the mornings, the nonsense voice that horses like, and the shifting slowed, and stopped.

The stable gate was in the far wall. It was barred on the inside with a beam. Beyond it was the bai’s main yard, and beyond that the big gate, and the village, and the road. The plan was simple. Lift the beam. Open the stable gate. Open the big gate, which would be barred too, but only with a beam, because who would steal from the soviet? Then drive the mares through and out and up the valley, all of them at once, at a gallop, in the dark, and let the bai’s men try to catch thirty-nine panicked horses in the night.
He had done it before. In 1920, outside Kokand, he had stolen a whole herd of remounts out of a basmachi camp in exactly this way.
He went along the wall with the boy behind him, among the mares, through the warm smell of them, and put his hands on the beam.
Kara-Jal screamed.

It was high and terrible, the sound a stallion makes when he is fighting. The black horse had smelled the strangers and the water and the cold, and he came round on his rope and reared and struck at the wall with his forefeet, and screamed again. The mares broke. They went every way at once in the dark, a great sliding surge of bodies, and Bayish was thrown against the gate and felt the beam go into his ribs, and somewhere a dog began to bark, and then all the dogs.
A light came on in the house.
“The beam!” Bayish shouted to the boy. “Lift it!”

They got it halfway. Then the door of the house opened and a man came out with a lantern, and behind him another with a shotgun, and behind them the bai’s son, in his shirt, shouting. The lantern swung. Bayish saw the boy’s face in it, white, with his mouth open, and saw the man with the shotgun see it too.
Bayish fired once over their heads, high, to make them drop, and they dropped, and the lantern went out.
“Back!” he said to the boy. “The aryk! Go!”

They ran. The boy went first, along the wall, among the mares. Bayish came behind him, and as he came someone fired from the house, a rifle this time, not the shotgun, and something hit him in the side like a thrown stone and spun him half round against the wall.
He did not fall. He was surprised by that, afterwards. He put his hand to his side and it came away wet and warm, and he thought, quite clearly, ribs, and kept going.
At the arch he looked back. The boy was not behind him.

He was in the middle of the yard, among the plunging mares, on his knees in the mud, and two of the bai’s men had him, one on each arm, the bad arm too, and the boy was not screaming, only twisting and kicking like a young horse at its first saddle. The lantern was alight again. In its light, standing on the step of the house in his good English coat with a carbine in his hands, quite calm, was Strelnikov.
He was looking straight at the arch.
Bayish lifted the carbine. He had a clear shot. Forty yards, lantern light, a still man on a step. He had made harder shots.
Then the bai’s man holding the boy’s good arm pulled the boy up and round, in front of himself, and held him there, and looked at the arch too.
Bayish lowered the carbine.

He went down into the water, on his back, under the wall, and out into the dark, with the cold of the aryk closing over his side like a hand, and the dogs still barking behind him, and the stallion still screaming, and over all of it, quite clearly, as he came out on the far side and began to run, the sound of Strelnikov’s voice saying something in Russian that might have been a laugh.

He did not remember getting to the sheepfold. He remembered the cold of the aryk, and running, and the dogs, and then he was in the ruined fold with his hands on the grey’s neck and his forehead against her shoulder, and she was standing quite still in the dark and letting him lean.
The boy’s pony was there, and Sapar’s pony, tied where they had left them. The boy was not.

Bayish stood there a while, breathing. His side was on fire. He opened his coat and his shirt and felt along the ribs with his fingers, and found the place where the bullet had gone along the bone, in at the front and out at the side, a long torn groove the length of his hand. Not deep. No rib broken, or he would not have been able to breathe like this. Bleeding, though. Bleeding a good deal, and his shirt was soaked and cold and stuck to him.

He tore the tail off the shirt and folded it into a pad and pressed it against the wound, and buttoned the coat over it tight. He untied the ponies and turned them loose. They would go home to the bai’s, or to Aimkan’s, or wherever ponies went. He could not lead them now.

Below in the village the dogs had stopped. There were lights in the bai’s compound, moving. Men with lanterns were coming out of the gate and spreading along the road, and two of them were coming up the hill.
Bayish got his foot into the stirrup on the third try, and pulled himself up into the saddle, and the grey moved off before he had asked her, up the hill and away from the lights, into the dark.

He let her choose the way. He had no choice about that. He could barely see, and he could not think very well, and when he tried to think, the thoughts went sideways and away from him like sheep on a hill. He held the saddle horn with one hand and his side with the other and let the mare go where she would.

She went up. Away from the river and the village and the road, up the long slope behind Kök-Saz, through the stubble terraces and then the thorn scrub and then the open hillside where the grass was burned and the wind came down cold off the tops. Somewhere along the way it began to snow again. He did not notice when. He noticed only that the darkness had gone grey and soft round him, and that there was snow on his knees, and on the mare’s mane, and on the strip of white felt that Aimkan had tied to her brow.
He thought about the boy.

He thought about the boy on his knees in the mud, between the bai’s men, twisting like a colt. He thought about the boy’s mother blowing on the fire, very carefully, and saying, So you had better not let him die. He thought about Ilyas in the dust.

He thought he had a clear shot at Strelnikov, and had not taken it, because of the boy, and that Strelnikov had known he would not take it. That was what the laugh had been: a man proved right about something he had hoped to be wrong about.
After a while he stopped thinking about anything at all.
When he woke, the grey had stopped.

He did not know how long he had been asleep, or if it had been sleep. He was still in the saddle, leaning forward over the horn, and his face was against the mare’s mane, and it was stiff with frost. The snow had stopped. The clouds had gone off somewhere, and there was a moon, almost full, high and white and very small, and in its light the whole hillside lay silver and silent round him, every stone and bush with its little cap of white.
He did not know where he was. Somewhere high. The valley of Kök-Saz was gone. Below him the hillside fell away into a fold of the mountains he did not recognise, a hollow full of shadow.
The grey was standing with her head down, looking at the snow in front of her.
He looked where she was looking.
There was a track in the snow.

One track. A single line of hoofprints, crossing the hillside in front of them from left to right and going on up the slope. The prints of a horse, unshod. Not a Chongtor. Bigger than that, longer in the stride, a tall horse, light on its feet, the prints clean-edged and sharp in the new snow, as if they had been made a minute ago. They came out of nowhere on his left, out of the unbroken snow of the hillside, and went away on his right, up over the shoulder of the hill and out of sight.
There was no rider’s track beside them. No man’s boots. Only the horse.
Bayish sat and looked at it for a long time.

He was a Party man. He was a Red cavalryman. He had read trails for twenty years. He knew that a single horse’s track in fresh snow on a moonlit hillside meant that a single horse had crossed the hillside since the snow stopped, and nothing more. A herder’s horse, strayed. A wild one, perhaps, from the old herds that ran on the high Chatkal. It meant nothing.
The grey lifted her head. She looked up the slope, where the track went, and her ears went forward.
Then she stepped into the track and began to follow it.

He did not stop her. He did not think he could have stopped her. He sat in the saddle with his hand on his side and the moon on the snow and let the mare carry him up the hillside, step by step, in the prints of the other horse, over the shoulder of the hill and down into the next hollow.
At the bottom of the hollow, among birches, there was a yurt. A white one. There was smoke coming out of the crown of it, straight up in the windless air, and the smell of juniper.
The track went across the snow toward the yurt and stopped at the door.
There was no horse there.

The man who came out of the yurt was very old. He was small and bent, with a white beard down to his chest and a long dark robe and a sheepskin over it, and on his chest, on a cord, a bare cross of carved walnut wood with three beads at the end of each arm, rising out of a flower.
He looked at the grey mare, and at the white felt on her brow, and at the man slumped in the saddle with his hand pressed to his side.
“Well,” he said. “Come in, then. Come in. You’re letting the cold in.”

His name was Father Mattai, and he was the priest of the upper Chatkal, and the yurt was his church. Bayish learned this in pieces, over a long time, between bouts of sleep, lying on a felt by the fire with his coat off and his shirt cut away. The old man washed the wound with warm water and salt. He sewed it up with a curved needle and a thread of white horsehair, quickly and neatly, the way a woman sews felt, while Bayish lay with his teeth shut and stared up at the crown of the yurt, where the smoke went out and the stars showed through. Then the old man smeared it with something that smelled of juniper and mutton fat, and bound it with clean linen, and made him drink a bowl of warm milk with honey in it.
“I don’t believe in any of this,” Bayish said, somewhere in the middle of it.
“No,” the old man agreed. “Drink your milk.”

The yurt was hung with felts, white ones, with the cross of the flower worked on them in red. At the far side, opposite the door, in the place where in a herder’s yurt the chest of honour would stand, there was a low table with a white cloth on it, and on the cloth a book with a wooden cover, and a small brass lamp, and a black walnut pot with a lid tied on with a thong.
“What’s in the pot?”

“Bread,” said Father Mattai. “Or the beginning of it. The mother leaven. The malka.” He looked at the pot. “My teacher gave it to me, and his teacher gave it to him. It goes back to the bread of Janyl, they say. I don’t know. I know it has never been let die.”

Bayish lay and looked at the pot. His mother had talked about the malka. In his village on the upper Talas they had not kept it any more, not since his grandmother’s time. His mother had been sorry about that.
“How did you find this place?” the old man asked. “Nobody comes here in the snow. Not even the shepherds.”
Bayish was silent.
“I followed a track,” he said at last.
Father Mattai sat back on his heels. He did not look surprised. He looked, if anything, a little sad.
“Yes,” he said. “Sometimes it’s like that.”
“There was no horse.”
“No,” said the priest. “There usually isn’t.”
He got up slowly, a hand on his knee, and went to the door of the yurt and lifted the felt and looked out at the moonlit snow. Then he let the felt fall and came back to the fire.

“Sometimes he comes for a soul,” he said. “To carry it home over the pass. Not tonight, I think. Your mare knows that.” He nodded toward the door, where the grey was standing outside under the birches. “What’s her name?”
“She doesn’t have one.”
“Everything has a name.”
Bayish thought about it.
“She never needed one,” he said.
The old man laughed, quietly, and for a moment, in the firelight, he looked much younger.
“No,” he said. “I don’t suppose she did.”

Bayish slept until noon. When he woke the priest was sitting by the door of the yurt in the thin sunlight with the wooden book on his knees, reading, moving his lips. The grey was grazing under the birches, pulling at the dry grass where the snow had melted off it. There was no track in the snow anywhere round the yurt except his own and the mare’s, coming down the hillside together.
He looked for a long time. Then he stopped looking.

“They’ll move the herd today,” Father Mattai said, without looking up from the book. “A shepherd came by at dawn. The bai is frightened. He’s sending the horses south with the Captain this afternoon. Over the walnut hills, toward the Fergana. Two days, perhaps three, to Kara-Jygach.” He turned a page. “And the boy goes with them.”
Bayish sat up too fast and the stitches pulled and he sat very still until the world steadied.
“Alive?”

“Alive. The bai’s no fool. He won’t kill a Chatkal boy in his own village, in front of the boy’s own people. He’d have half the valley at his gate.” The priest closed the book. “No. He’ll send him with the herd. As a hostage, in case the man who came under the wall tries again. And when they get to Kara-Jygach, and the Captain has his gold, then perhaps there’s an accident on a mountain path. Boys fall off mountains. Everybody knows that.”
Bayish was already reaching for his shirt.
“You’ll open those stitches,” the priest said, without getting up.
“Then you’ll have to sew them again.”

Father Mattai got up, and went to the low table with the white cloth, and untied the thong on the walnut pot, and took a pinch of something from inside it, a small grey lump of dough, and wrapped it in a scrap of white felt and tied it with a white thread, and came back and put it into Bayish’s hand.

“It’s given,” the priest said. “Never sold. To brides. To new priests. To the head of a family when the herd divides.” He closed Bayish’s fingers over it. “And to men who are going a long way and might not come back. Keep it warm. Feed it if you can. If you can’t, it doesn’t matter. Somebody will find it.”
“I’m a Party man.”
“So you keep telling me,” said Father Mattai. “Go on. Your mare’s waiting.”
