The walnut forest began a day’s ride south of the priest’s yurt, where the Chatkal hills fold down toward the Fergana and the air goes soft and the snow gives out.

Bayish came into it in the late afternoon, out of the high bare country, down a long slope of dead bracken, and the trees closed over him all at once like water. They were old trees, older than anything he had seen on the Talas, with trunks a man could not put his arms round and great grey branches that went out and out over the slope and met the branches of the next tree, so that the light came down green and gold and broken, and the ground was soft and brown with fallen leaves and the husks of walnuts, black and split. It smelled bitter and clean, of leaf-rot and green walnut and woodsmoke from somewhere far off.

The herd’s trail went through it like a river through a reed bed. Thirty-nine mares and the black stallion, eight or nine men, and now the bai’s people too, a dozen riders by the look of it, had come down this slope that morning and torn a wide brown road through the leaves, and broken branches, and left their dung in heaps. A child could have followed it.
That was what worried him.

He rode slowly, with the carbine across the saddle in front of him and his side stiff and burning under the priest’s linen. He had opened two of the stitches getting into the saddle that morning, as the priest had said he would, and felt them go, and said nothing. The bleeding had stopped again. He did not think about it.
The grey went quietly through the leaves with her ears moving. The white felt was still on her brow, a little grey now with dirt. Twice he had thought about taking it off, and twice he had not.
At the bottom of the slope, where a stream came down through the trees in a little ravine, he found the third mare.

She was lying in the stream with her head on the bank, as if she had lain down to drink and not got up. A bay, heavy in foal, near her time. There was no wound on her. She had simply been driven too far too fast, down off the mountain and through the forest, with the foal pulling at her from inside, and somewhere on the slope her heart had given out, and they had left her where she fell.
The foal had moved once inside her as Bayish knelt there. He felt it under his hand. Then it was still.

He did not shoot her. There was no need. He stayed there a while with his hand on her flank, and the stream going past, and the walnut leaves coming down one by one through the green light and settling on the water.
Thirty-eight.

He thought of Pavlov, standing in the empty corral with his rifle he did not know how to hold. He thought of Kalmurat, who had bred some of these mares from foals and knew all their names. He thought: they don’t care. Kalmurat had said it. They’re not selling foals. They’re selling horses.
He got up and went on.
Half a mile further on, the trail split.

It was very well done. Bayish gave Strelnikov that, as he had given the bai his calm. The trail came down the stream valley to a place where the trees opened into a long glade, and there, on a bare patch of stony ground where the leaves had blown away, it divided. One road went on south, down the valley. The other turned east, up a side ravine toward the higher ground. Both were wide. Both were trampled by many hooves. Both had fresh dung on them.
And in the soft earth at the edge of the eastern trail, clear as a signature, the crooked half-moon of the big bay.
Bayish sat the grey at the fork and read it.

The east trail went up. Up toward the high passes, toward the Kökjal country and the long way round to China. A man who wanted to sell his horses on the Fergana side and be gone would not go that way. But a man who knew he was being followed, by someone who knew his horse’s track, might send his horse that way, and go the other.
He got down. He went along the eastern trail on foot, bent over, for fifty yards, reading it. Then he came back and did the same on the southern one.
It took him a quarter of an hour. When he had finished he stood in the glade with the leaves coming down round him, and almost smiled.

The eastern trail was a dozen horses. No more. Chongtor ponies, mostly, ridden, and a few loose ones driven ahead, and something dragged behind them, branches perhaps, to churn the ground and make it look like more. The dung was fresh, but there was not enough of it. And the half-moon track of the big bay was there, sharp and crooked, but too shallow. The bay was being led. Nobody was riding him. A big horse with a man on him sinks deep in soft ground. This one was walking light, like a horse in a paddock.

The southern trail was the herd. Thirty-eight mares in foal, heavy, slow, their tracks deep and close together. Dung in long trails, the loose dung of tired horses. And among the mares, here and there, the prints of the riders’ ponies, and once, in a patch of mud by a spring, the long narrow print of a riding boot. A good boot, mended by someone who knew boots.
Strelnikov had put his horse on the decoy and gone with the herd on something else.
“You clever bastard,” Bayish said aloud, to the glade, and the grey turned her head and looked at him.
He found the boy’s sign a mile down the southern trail.

It was a strip of cloth, tied to a low branch at the height of a rider’s hand. Grey cloth, dirty, torn from a shirt. Bayish knew the shirt. He had cut the sleeve of it on the Kenkol to get at the boy’s arm.
He sat and looked at it, and had to wait a while before he could ride on.

A mile further on there was another. Then, at a stream crossing, a walnut twig broken and laid across a stone, pointing down the valley. Then another strip of cloth, very small this time, as if the boy were running out of shirt. They were not leading him anywhere. He did not need leading. The herd’s trail was a road.
They were a message that the boy was alive, and knew he was being followed, and was not afraid.
Or was afraid, and tying them anyway.
At dusk he came to a walnut-gatherers’ camp.

It was in a clearing among the big trees: two felt tents and a brushwood shelter and a fire, and sacks of walnuts heaped against a log, and children, and a dog that came out barking and then thought better of it. A man got up from the fire with an axe in his hand, and then saw the carbine across Bayish’s saddle, and put the axe down slowly, the way Aimkan had put down her ladle.

They were Fergana people, from the hill villages below. Muslims, by the man’s skullcap and the women’s dress and the way the old woman by the fire said bismillah under her breath when she saw him. They had come up into the forest, as they did every autumn, to gather the walnuts on the family’s plot, and they would be here another two weeks, until the first big snow drove them down.

They had seen the herd. Of course they had seen it. It had come through the edge of their plot at midday, a river of horses, and men with rifles, and the man with the axe had stood in front of his children and not said a word while they went past.
“Russians?” he asked Bayish. “Soldiers?”
“Thieves.”

The man looked at him. Then he said something to his wife, and she brought bread, round and flat and still warm from the ashes, and a bowl of walnuts, and a pot of tea, and set them on a felt by the fire, and the man waved Bayish to it.
Bayish sat. He had not known how hungry he was until he smelled the bread.

The old woman watched him eat. She was very old, older than the priest, with a face like a dried apple and eyes that missed nothing. When he had finished, she leaned forward and pointed at the grey mare, who was standing by the tents with the white felt on her brow, and said something to her son in the Fergana speech, quickly, too quick for Bayish to follow.
The son looked uncomfortable. “My mother says,” he said, “that the mare has been blessed. By the Christians. The ones up in the mountains.”
“Yes,” said Bayish. There was no point in saying otherwise.
The old woman said something else.

“She says,” said the son, “that in the summer of the troubles, when she was a girl, her father went over the mountain to the Chatkal with the soldiers behind him, and the Christian people up there hid him in their houses for a week and fed him and did not tell. She says it doesn’t matter what God put the felt on the mare. She says a blessing is a blessing.” He hesitated. “She says the men who went past today are not blessed by anybody.”
The old woman nodded firmly and sat back.
“Where are they going?” Bayish asked.
The man’s face closed a little. “South. Down to Kara-Jygach. To the Kurbashi’s camp.”
“You know the Kurbashi?”

“Everybody knows the Kurbashi.” The man looked at the sacks of walnuts heaped against the log. “Every autumn his men come up here and take one sack in five. For the cause, they say. Before, it was for Islam. Now it is just for the cause.” He shrugged. “The Soviets came last year and said the Kurbashi was finished. The Kurbashi is not finished. The Kurbashi is in Kara-Jygach with eighty men, and he takes one sack in five.”
“Eighty.”
“Perhaps more. Perhaps fewer. They come and go.”
Bayish looked into the fire.
Eighty men. And the Captain’s eight, and the bai’s dozen. One man with a carbine and a hundred and fourteen rounds, and a hole in his side, and a pinch of bread in a scrap of felt.
The old woman leaned forward again and said something, and this time she said it slowly, looking straight at him, so that he would understand.

“She says,” said her son, “there are soldiers coming. Real ones. Russian ones, from the Talas side. Six of them, on big horses. Her nephew saw them yesterday at the top of the forest, coming down your way. She says you should wait for them.”
Bayish looked at the old woman. She looked back at him with her dried-apple face and did not blink.
“Thank you, mother,” he said.
He did not say whether he would wait.

He woke in the middle of the night and the son was gone from the fire. Bayish lay still under his coat and watched him go, a dark shape moving away down the hill through the walnut trees toward the south, with an empty sack over his shoulder.
One sack in five, the man had said. A family that pays the Kurbashi a fifth of its walnuts pays him in other ways too.
Bayish did not stop him. In the morning the son was back by the fire, blowing on the embers, and would not meet his eye. The old woman gave Bayish bread for the road and said nothing at all.
They caught him at noon the next day, at a ford, because he let them.

He heard them a long way off, the way you hear any Russian cavalry in mountains: the clink of bits and the creak of good leather, and big shod hooves on stones, and a man’s voice saying something sharp and another man laughing. He could have gone up into the trees and let them pass. He sat the grey in the middle of the ford instead, with the water running round her knees and the carbine across the saddle, and waited.

There were six of them, as the old woman had said, on tall Don horses, bays and chestnuts, sweating and blowing from the hill. Five men in long grey coats with the red star on their caps and rifles slung, and in front, on the best horse, a young man with a leather coat and a Mauser pistol in a wooden holster on his hip and a face that had been shaved that morning in cold water by a man who believed in shaving.
He pulled up at the edge of the ford and looked at Bayish, and his hand went to the holster and stayed there.
“Who are you?”
“Bayish Kenje uulu. Chong-Talas stud.”
The young man’s face changed. “The horse-breaker,” he said. “The one who went after them alone.”
“Yes.”
“Get down off that horse.”
His name was Ivanchuk, Lieutenant, of the OGPU, Talas district detachment, and he was twenty-six years old and from a village near Poltava, and he was very angry.
“You went over the Kenkol after an armed counter-revolutionary band,” Ivanchuk said. “Alone. Without orders. Without informing the competent organs.”
“The competent organs were mending a lorry in Kara-Buura.”

“Because your director telephoned Talas and said horse thieves. Horse thieves! It took him a second call to mention a White officer.” He looked down at his boots, scraped grey to the ankle. “I lost a horse on your scree. A good one.”

Bayish stood in the shallows with the water round his boots and let him be angry. A divisional commissar had shouted at him for an hour once, outside Kokand in 1920, and then given him a medal. It passed.
“That weapon,” Ivanchuk said, pointing at the carbine. “Where did you get it?”
“The Fergana. In ’21.”
“Is it registered?”
“No.”
“Then it’s illegal. You’re carrying an illegal weapon in a border zone. Give it to me.”
Bayish did not move.
The five men behind the lieutenant had gone quiet. One of them, a thickset man with a broad Kazakh face and a sergeant’s stripes, sat his horse very still and watched Bayish’s hands.
“Comrade Lieutenant,” Bayish said. “I’ll give you something else first.”
He reached slowly into his coat, slowly enough that the sergeant could see what he was doing, and took out the Party card, and held it out.

Ivanchuk took it. He opened it and read it. He read it twice before he looked up, and something in his face shifted, not much, the way ice shifts on a river in March before anything has really happened.
“Six years,” he said.
“Six years.”
“And before that?”

“The Iradi volunteer horse, in ’19. Then the Turkestan Front, scouts. The Fergana. Kokand. Andijan.” Bayish held out his hand, and Ivanchuk, after a moment, gave the card back. “I know the Black Kurbashi. I’ve fought him. I know Strelnikov. I know his horse. I’ve followed it twice now.” He put the card away. “You can have my carbine, Comrade Lieutenant. When the mares are back at Chong-Talas. Until then I’ll keep it, and you can write me up in your report, and I’ll sign it.”
They had the argument properly that evening, at the camp, after the men had seen to the horses.

Ivanchuk spread an old survey sheet on a flat stone and weighted the corners with cartridges. “We follow them to Kara-Jygach,” he said, and drew a neat line with his pencil. “We confirm the location. Two men ride back to Talas. The organs request a detachment from the Fergana garrison, with a machine-gun section.” The pencil made a ring round Kara-Jygach. “Then we liquidate the bandit formation.”
“How long?” Bayish said.
Ivanchuk calculated. “Two weeks. Perhaps three.”
“In three weeks the mares will be in Kashgar. Or in the Kurbashi’s cooking pots.”

“Then they’ll be in Kashgar. They’re horses.” Ivanchuk looked at him across the fire. “I have six men, comrade. You have one carbine and a hole in your side. They have eighty. What do you want me to do? Charge?”
“No.”
“Then what?”

Bayish looked into the fire. He could not have explained it. That was the trouble. He could have explained it to Kalmurat, or to the priest, or to the boy’s mother. He could not explain it to a young man from Poltava with a map and a pencil and a plan.

“There’s a boy with them,” he said instead. “A hostage. Sixteen years old. From the Chatkal. If the Red Army comes up that valley with a machine-gun section, the first thing anybody does is cut his throat.”
“A boy.” Ivanchuk frowned. “What boy? There’s nothing in the report about a boy.”
“There’s nothing in the report about anything.”
Bayish took the strip of grey cloth out of his pocket, the last one he had found, the small one, and put it on the map by the fire, on top of the place marked Kara-Jygach.

“He’s been leaving me these,” he said. “All the way down through the forest. Every mile. With his hands tied and a bullet hole in his arm that I put there. So that I’d know he was alive.” He looked up. “You go back to Talas and write your report, Comrade Lieutenant. I’m going to Kara-Jygach.”
Ivanchuk picked up the strip of cloth and turned it over in his fingers.
“You’ll get them all killed,” he said at last. “The boy. Yourself. The mares. All of them.”
“Then come and stop me.”
The sergeant with the Kazakh face, who had been sitting a little way off pretending to clean his rifle, laughed once, very quietly, and turned it into a cough.
Later, when the men were asleep, Ivanchuk came and sat down by Bayish at the edge of the firelight, where Bayish was sitting with his back against a walnut tree and the carbine across his knees.
For a while he only sat and watched the grey mare, who was standing a little apart from the big Don horses, asleep on her feet, with the white felt pale on her brow in the dark.
“What’s that?” he said at last. “On her head.”
“A woman tied it there.”
“For what?”

“Superstition,” Ivanchuk said, not unkindly. “Up here they’re full of it. In the villages. They tie rags to trees, they pour milk on stones. They think a white horse comes down off the mountains.” He shook his head. “In ten years it’ll all be gone. Electricity. Schools. Tractors. In ten years every child in the Chatkal will read Lenin, and no one will remember any of it.”
“Perhaps.”
“You don’t believe in it.”
“No.”
“Then why don’t you take it off?”
Bayish thought about that. The fire had burned down to embers. Somewhere above them in the walnut trees an owl was calling, two notes, over and over.

“Because a woman tied it there,” he said, “whose husband died on the ice above the Kökjal, and whose son I shot. And I told her I’d bring him back.” He looked at the young man. “If I bring him back, she can take it off herself.”
Ivanchuk said nothing. After a while he got up and went back to his blanket.

But in the morning, when Bayish saddled the grey, the lieutenant came over and stood by him and watched, and when Bayish swung up into the saddle, Ivanchuk said, “The sergeant thinks you know what you’re doing.”
“Does he.”

“Sergeant Zhakupov was at Kokand too. In 1920. He says he remembers a scout who stole a whole herd of remounts out of a basmachi camp in one night, and the basmachi never found out how.” The young man’s face was quite expressionless. “He says the scout rode a bay with a white face.”
Bayish looked over at the sergeant, who was tightening his own girth and did not look up.
“It was a long time ago,” he said.
“Yes,” said Ivanchuk. He swung up onto the big Don bay. “We’ll go together, then. As far as Kara-Jygach. Then we’ll see.” He gathered his reins. “You’ll keep the carbine. For now. I’ll write you up.”
“I’ll sign it.”

They rode south all that day, out of the walnut forest and down into the dry hills above the Fergana, where the trees gave out and the slopes were brown and bare and cut by deep stony ravines, and the light was hard and white and went on for ever.

In the middle of the afternoon Zhakupov brought his big Don horse up level with the grey, on her off side, and rode there for a while without saying anything. Ivanchuk was out in front with two of the privates, studying the land through his field glasses and making marks on his map. The sergeant watched him do it for some time.
“The lieutenant told you,” he said at last, in Kazakh, “that I remember Kokand.”
“He did.”
“He has it wrong.” Zhakupov shifted the rifle across his saddle. “I never saw the scout’s face. What I remember is the horse lines.”
Bayish looked at him.

“I was sixteen,” the sergeant said. “From the lower Chu. My father had a few horses and a few sheep and a debt, like everybody. In the spring of 1920 a kurbashi came through with his men and took the horses, and took me to look after them. That was how it was done then. They took the boys who could ride, and gave them an old rifle and the night watch on the horse lines, and if the horses were stolen, they beat the boy.” He said it without any feeling at all, the way Aimkan had told about the ice. “So I was on the horse lines outside Kokand. With an old Berdan. On the night the remounts went.”
They rode on a little way. The grey’s ears had turned back toward the sergeant’s voice.

“It was very dark,” Zhakupov said. “No moon. About two in the morning. I was sitting on a saddle at the end of the line, half asleep, and I heard a man talking. Low. Not words. Nonsense. The sounds you make to a horse in the morning when you come into the yard, so she knows who it is.” He glanced across. “My grandmother talked like that to the mares at milking. I had not heard it since I was small. So I sat on the saddle and listened, and I thought I was dreaming about my grandmother.”
“And then?”

“And then I saw him. A shape, walking down the line in the dark, with his hand on each horse as he went by. Cutting the picket ropes. One, and then the next, and then the next. Quite slowly. Talking to them the whole time.” The sergeant was silent for a moment. “I had the Berdan on him from the third horse to the last. Forty yards. I could not have missed.”
“Why didn’t you shoot?”
Zhakupov thought about it, as if nobody had ever asked him before, and perhaps nobody had.

“Because the horses were not afraid of him,” he said. “Two hundred horses, in the dark, with a stranger among them, cutting their ropes. And not one of them pulled back or made a sound. They put their heads down to him as he went by, like they were in their own yard.” He shrugged, a small movement of the big shoulders. “I was sixteen. I thought: a man the horses are not afraid of is not a man I want to kill. So I sat on my saddle and watched him take them all away into the dark, and in the morning the kurbashi beat me with a whip until I could not stand. A week later I walked into Kokand and joined the Reds.”
He looked across at Bayish, and for the first time since the ford his broad face showed something that was nearly a smile.
“So you see, comrade,” he said. “I have been following you for five years. You just did not know it.”
Bayish rode for a while without answering. He looked at the grey’s ears, and the brown hills going on and on ahead of them in the hard white light.
“It was a long time ago,” he said.
“Not so long,” said Zhakupov, and touched his heel to the big Don horse, and went forward to see what the lieutenant was writing on his map.
Late in the afternoon, from the top of a long ridge, Bayish pulled up and pointed.

Far off, on the edge of the hills, where they broke down in cliffs and gullies toward the great flat haze of the valley, there was a fold in the land, and in the fold there were trees, poplars and willows, the green of water. And above the trees, going up thin and straight into the evening, smoke. Many fires. More than he could count.
“Kara-Jygach,” said Sergeant Zhakupov, beside him.
Ivanchuk took out his field glasses and swept the fold from end to end.
“Eighty,” he said at last, quietly. “At least.”
Bayish said nothing. He was looking at the gorge.

Between the ridge where they sat and the fold with the smoke in it, there was only one way down. A narrow ravine, deep and steep-sided, with a dry stream bed at the bottom and a path along it. The herd’s trail went down into it and did not come out until the far end, where the poplars began.
It was a very good place for an ambush.

He had seen a great many places like it in the Fergana. He had ridden into some of them. The ones who rode out again were the ones who had looked at the walls of the ravine first and asked themselves where they would put men, if they were the other side.
He sat on the ridge in the last of the light and looked at the walls of the ravine, and asked himself.
“Nobody rides into that gorge in daylight,” Bayish said.

Ivanchuk looked up from his map. They were sitting below the crest of the ridge, out of sight of the fold and the smoke, in the last grey light, with the horses picketed behind them in a hollow and the men eating cold bread. The lieutenant had marked the gorge on the map with his pencil, a neat little line with an arrow at the end of it.
“It’s the only way in.”

“It’s the only way in for horses. It’s not the only way in for men.” Bayish pointed up at the dark rim of the ravine, where it came out against the sky on either side. “If I were the Kurbashi, I’d have three men up there on each side. Maybe four. Behind the rocks, at the narrow place, halfway down, where the path goes close under the west wall. They let the column into the narrow place, and then they shoot the first horse and the last horse, and then they shoot everything in between.”
“You don’t know there’s anyone up there.”
“No.”
“Then how...”
“Because it’s what I’d do.”
Ivanchuk stared at him. Then he turned to Sergeant Zhakupov, who was sitting on a rock nearby, chewing, and looking at nothing.
“Sergeant?”
Zhakupov swallowed. “It’s what I’d do too, Comrade Lieutenant.”

They argued about it for an hour. In the end it was decided the way most things are decided in the army, which is that the officer decided, and the officer was twenty-six and from Poltava and had his orders, and his orders said nothing about scouts going up cliffs in the dark on their own initiative. They would go down the gorge at first light, in column, with intervals of twenty paces, rifles ready, and if they were fired on, they would return fire and push through to the far end at a gallop.
“And you,” Ivanchuk said to Bayish, “will ride with the column. Where I can see you.”
“No,” said Bayish.
He said it quite gently. Ivanchuk opened his mouth, and then shut it.

“I’m going up the west rim tonight,” Bayish said. “On foot. Before you go in. If there’s nobody there, I’ll come down to the far end and wait for you under the poplars, and you can put me under arrest. If there is somebody there...” He shrugged. “Then you’ll hear.”

He got up, and took the carbine, and went to the grey in the hollow, and stood with her a moment, rubbing her face. She pushed her nose against his chest. He took the white felt off her brow, carefully, unpicking Aimkan’s knot with his fingers, and folded it, and put it in the inside pocket of his coat, with the Party card and the priest’s pinch of bread.
“Sergeant,” he said, without turning round. “Look after my mare.”
“I will,” said Zhakupov.

It took him four hours to get up the west rim of the gorge in the dark. He went a long way round, back along the ridge and then out to the west and down into a side gully that he had marked from the crest in the last of the light, and up its far side, on hands and knees much of the time, with the carbine slung across his back and his side tearing at every handhold. Twice he had to stop and lie flat on the cold stone until the world stopped turning. Once a stone went out from under his foot and went down into the dark, knocking from rock to rock, and he lay with his face against the rock for ten minutes, not breathing, listening, and nothing happened.
By three in the morning he was on the rim. By four he had found them.

There were three. He found them by their smell before anything else: tobacco and sheep-fat and wet felt. They were in a nest of boulders at the narrow place, exactly where he would have put them, lying in their coats and blankets with their rifles beside them, one awake and two asleep. Across the gorge, on the far rim, against the first faint grey of the sky, he thought he could see the shapes of more boulders, and perhaps a man among them, and perhaps not.
He lay forty yards behind the three on the west rim, in a crack between two stones, and waited for the light.

It came slowly, grey and then white, filling the gorge from the top down, like water poured into a bowl. Below him lay the dry stream bed and the path along it, pale among the stones. Then the far rim came clear, and on it, as he had thought, three more men, in a line of rocks a little higher than his own.

The man on watch in front of him woke the other two with his foot. They sat up and rubbed their faces and took up their rifles and lay down behind the boulders facing the gorge, and one of them lit a pipe, and the smoke went up thin and blue in the cold.
Then, far up the gorge, from the north, Bayish heard horses.

The column came down into the ravine at a walk, as Ivanchuk had said. Six big horses, twenty paces apart, the men in their grey coats with their rifles across their saddles, looking up at the walls. The lieutenant rode second, behind a private on a chestnut. Zhakupov rode last, leading the grey mare on a rope. She came quietly behind his big Don horse, with her wall eye rolling up at the cliffs, and Bayish lay in his crack in the rock and watched her come and thought, I should not have let her go down there, and could do nothing about it.
The three men in front of him had seen the column. They were very still. The one with the pipe had put it down on the rock. They were waiting for the first horse to reach the narrow place.

Bayish looked across the gorge at the far rim, and the three men there, and calculated. Forty yards to the ones in front of him. A hundred and fifty across to the others. He could take the three in front. He could take them before they knew he was there. But the moment he fired, the three on the far rim would fire too, at the column, down into the narrow place, and the column would be caught in the open.
Unless he fired first. Before the column was in the narrow place. Before they were ready.
He did not wait any longer.

He shot the man with the pipe first, through the back, and the man pitched forward over his rifle. The second man came up on his knees and turned, and Bayish shot him too. The third one was quicker. He rolled into the boulders and fired once, wild, at the crack in the rocks, and the bullet went off the stone a foot above Bayish’s head and away into the sky. Then he ran. He ran along the rim, crouched over, away toward the south, toward the fold and the smoke, and Bayish fired once after him and missed, and let him go, because by then the far rim was firing.

They fired at the column, as he had known they would. But the column was not in the narrow place yet. It was a hundred yards short of it, in the open, and the first volley came too early and too high, and Bayish heard Ivanchuk’s voice come up out of the gorge, very loud and quite steady: “Dismount! Cover! Return fire!”

The big horses plunged and reared. One went down, a chestnut, with a private still half in the saddle. The rest of the men were off their horses and in among the stones of the stream bed, firing up at the far rim. It was the shooting of men lying on their backs among rocks, firing at a cliff a hundred feet above them.
Bayish was not on his back.

He came out of his crack and ran along the west rim to the nest of boulders where the three men had been, and lay down behind the dead man with the pipe, and laid the carbine on the rock, and looked across the gorge.

A hundred and fifty yards. A little downhill. No wind. Three men behind rocks, with their heads and shoulders showing as they fired down into the gorge, and not one of them looking across at the other rim, where their own people were.
He took them one at a time.

The first he hit in the shoulder, and the man dropped his rifle over the cliff and went down behind his rock. The second he missed, and missed again, and then hit as the man rose to see where the shots were coming from. The third saw him. He swung his rifle round and they fired at the same moment, and something plucked at Bayish’s sleeve, and the man on the far rim sat down very suddenly and did not get up.
Then it was quiet.

Down in the gorge a horse was screaming. Somebody was shouting in Russian, over and over, a name. Sokolov. Sokolov. Bayish lay on the rock with his cheek against the cold stock of the carbine and his side burning like a coal, and counted his cartridges, because it was something to do with his hands. He had fired eight. He had a hundred and six left. It had taken perhaps two minutes.
When he came down into the gorge the sun was up, and it was over.

Two of Ivanchuk’s men were dead. Sokolov, a boy from Tver with fair hair, had been in the saddle of the chestnut when it went down, and the first volley had taken him through the chest. Bekov, a Tatar from Kazan, had been hit in the head as he dismounted, and was lying among the stones of the stream bed with his rifle still in his hands. The chestnut was dead. A second horse was down with a broken leg, and Zhakupov had shot it.

Ivanchuk was sitting against a boulder with his leather coat open and his right trouser leg cut away and a field dressing on his thigh, already soaking through red. He was very white. He watched Bayish come down the last of the slope and pick his way through the stones toward him, and waited until Bayish was standing over him.
“Two,” he said. “Two of mine.”
“Yes.”
“If we’d been in the narrow place...”
“Yes.”
Ivanchuk looked away down the gorge, toward the far end, where the poplars began and the smoke of the Kurbashi’s camp went up into the clear morning. His jaw was working.
“You were right,” he said at last. “Write that in your report. I’ll sign it.”

The grey mare was standing by Zhakupov’s horse at the side of the path, on her rope, untouched. When she saw Bayish she lifted her head and called to him, once, a short low sound, and he went to her and put his hand on her neck and stood there, and the sergeant looked at the two of them and turned away and busied himself with a girth.

They had one prisoner. He was the man Bayish had hit in the shoulder on the far rim. Two of the privates had climbed up after the shooting stopped and dragged him down. He was a thin hill man of thirty or so, with a scrubby beard and terrified eyes, and he sat on a stone with his arm hanging and answered everything Zhakupov asked him, very fast, in the Fergana speech.

Yes, the Kurbashi was at Kara-Jygach. Yes, the horses had come in yesterday evening. The Captain had come with them, and the bai’s men, and they were all in the camp under the poplars by the spring. Eighty men, perhaps more. The Kurbashi and the Captain were to sit together tonight and agree a price. The money was to be paid tomorrow at dawn, in gold, and the bai’s men would go home, and the Captain would go east toward China with his share, and the horses would go to the Kurbashi.
“And the boy?” Bayish said. “The Chatkal boy. With the bad arm.”
The prisoner looked at him. “The Captain keeps him. In his own tent. With a rope on his foot.” He hesitated. “The Captain says he is a guarantee.”
“Of what?”
The man shrugged with his good shoulder. “Of you, I think.”

Ivanchuk could not ride. Zhakupov said it, and Ivanchuk said it himself, after he had tried to stand and fallen back against the boulder with his face grey and sweating. The bullet was still in his thigh. It had missed the bone and the big vessel, or he would be dead already, but it needed a surgeon, and the nearest surgeon was in Namangan, two days down in the valley.
“Then we go back,” Ivanchuk said. “We go back and get the detachment. There’s nothing else. I have three men who can fight. You have one carbine.”

“The Kurbashi heard the shooting,” Bayish said. “He’ll have every man in the camp up by now. By the time your detachment gets here, the mares will be gone, and so will Strelnikov, and the boy will be at the bottom of a cliff.”
“Then what?” The lieutenant’s voice cracked. “What do you want? Tell me what you want.”
Bayish looked down the gorge at the smoke.
“I’m going to walk into his camp,” he said, “tonight. Alone. Without the carbine. As a guest.”
There was a silence in the gorge. Even the privates who were digging in the stony ground for the two dead men stopped digging.
“He’ll kill you,” Ivanchuk said.
“No. He won’t. Not under his own roof.” Bayish turned to the prisoner on his stone. “Tell me. Is the Kurbashi a man of the old law? Does he keep the guest?”
The prisoner’s eyes went to the sergeant, and then back to Bayish, and he nodded, once.
“The Kurbashi keeps the guest,” he said. “Three days. Even an enemy. Even a Russian.” He swallowed. “After three days, he kills them.”
“Three days is plenty,” said Bayish.
He went down the last of the gorge at sunset, on foot, leading the grey, with his hands empty and his coat open so that anyone could see there was no pistol in his belt.

The carbine stayed behind with Zhakupov. So did the hundred and six rounds. Bayish had handed them over without a word, and the sergeant had taken them without a word, and then, when Bayish turned to go, had said in Kazakh, very low, so that the lieutenant would not hear: If you are not back by the second dawn, I will come in after you, and so will these two boys, and we will all die very stupidly together. And Bayish had said, in the same language, Then I’d better be back.

At the far end of the gorge the path came out of the rocks into a long sloping meadow with poplars along the bottom of it, where a spring came out of the hill and spread into a marsh of reeds and willows. The camp was there. Tents and brushwood shelters and horse lines all along the edge of the trees, and fires, many fires, and men round them. More than eighty. A hundred, perhaps.
They saw him a long way off. He had meant them to.

By the time he was halfway down the meadow there were twenty men standing at the edge of the camp, with rifles, watching him come. By the time he reached the first fire there were fifty. Nobody raised a rifle. Nobody spoke. They simply stood, and looked at him, and at the wall-eyed grey mare, and let him walk in among them, and closed up behind him, so that by the time he stopped in the middle of the camp, by the biggest fire, he was standing in a ring of men three deep with his back to nothing at all.
He stood there, and waited.

The Black Kurbashi was not black. Bayish had never seen him close, in 1921. He had imagined something, a big man, a beard, a face like a hawk. The man who came out of the largest tent and stood in the firelight was small and neat and grey-haired, perhaps sixty, with a short white beard and a quilted coat of dark blue silk and a turban wound small and tight, and a face like a schoolmaster’s, mild and tired and very intelligent.
He studied Bayish. Then his eyes went to the grey mare.

“I know you,” he said. He spoke the Fergana Iradi, softly, with the Uzbek in it. “Not your face. Your way of standing. You were the scout. In the summer of ’21. In the valleys above Andijan.” He tilted his head. “My men called you the Shadow. They used to say that if the Shadow was in front of a Red patrol, there was no point in laying an ambush, because he would be sitting on top of it when it went off.”
“Your men exaggerated.”

“Did they?” The Kurbashi smiled very slightly. “I have six men on the rims of Kara-Jygach who would tell you otherwise. Or I would have, if four of them were not dead and the fifth were not in the hands of the OGPU.” He folded his hands inside his sleeves. “And now you walk into my camp. With no rifle. At sunset. Why?”
“I’ve come as a guest,” Bayish said. “To ask the master of the house for the price of forty horses.”

It was the old form of words. The one that a man used on the steppe, long ago, when he came to another man’s camp to talk about a theft, or a debt, or a death, and wanted it known that he had come to talk and not to fight. Bayish had heard his grandfather use it once, when he was a small boy, at a camp on the upper Talas, and had not thought of it since. He was surprised the words were still there when he reached for them.
The Kurbashi’s face did not change. But round the fire, in the ring of men, there was a sound, a kind of low murmur, like wind going over long grass.
“Thirty-eight,” the Kurbashi said. “There are thirty-eight. I counted them myself.” He turned and spoke over his shoulder, to a boy by the tent. “Bring tea. And bring the Captain.”

They sat on a felt by the fire, the three of them, with the tea between them, and the ring of men standing round at a distance, listening. Strelnikov had come out of his tent in his good English coat and looked at Bayish and laughed, as he had laughed at Kök-Saz, softly, without much pleasure, and sat down.
“I told you,” he said in Russian, to the Kurbashi. “Didn’t I tell you? He walks into things. It’s a disease.”
“Speak Iradi,” said the Kurbashi mildly. “My men like to know what is being said.”

Strelnikov shrugged and switched. “He walks into things,” he said again. “He walked into my camp on the Kenkol. He walked into Abdyrakhman’s house at Kök-Saz. Now he walks into yours. One day he will walk into something he can’t walk out of.” He took a glass of tea. “Possibly tonight.”
The Kurbashi ignored him. He looked at Bayish.
“You came to ask a price,” he said. “Ask.”
Bayish put his tea down untouched.
“The mares are from the state stud at Chong-Talas,” he said. “Every one of them is in foal to the black stallion.”
The Kurbashi’s glass stopped on its way to his mouth.

“Every one of them is in a book in Pavlov’s office,” Bayish said. “Her colour, her marks, her name. There’s a copy in Tashkent, at the remount service.” He waited. Somewhere in the ring of men somebody coughed. “There isn’t a dealer between here and Kashgar who won’t know a Chong-Talas mare when he sees one. They’re the best riding horses in Turkestan. That’s why he stole them.” He nodded at Strelnikov. “It’s also why you can’t keep them.”
The Kurbashi set the glass down without drinking. He was looking at Strelnikov now.

“There’s a Red Army garrison at Namangan,” Bayish said. “Two days’ ride. There’s an OGPU lieutenant up in your gorge with a bullet in his leg who is going to be very angry when he gets to a surgeon, and there are two dead men up there who were shot by your pickets. You can kill me tonight. But the lieutenant knows I’m here. If I don’t come back, he goes down to Namangan, and in a week there will be a regiment of Red cavalry in Kara-Jygach, with guns. Not for me. For the mares.” He paused. “And for you. Because you bought them.”
There was a long silence round the fire.

“That’s very good,” said Strelnikov at last, admiringly. “That’s very good indeed. Did you think of all that yourself, or did the lieutenant help?” He turned to the Kurbashi. “He’s bluffing. The lieutenant’s dying in the gorge. Nobody’s going to Namangan. Nobody in Tashkent cares about forty mares. Pay me, and I’ll be gone at dawn, and you can do what you like with this one.”
The Kurbashi did not answer at once. He drank his tea, slowly, looking into the fire. When he spoke, he did not speak to Strelnikov.

“You told me,” he said, “that these were horses from a bai’s herd in the Chatkal. Surplus. With papers. You told me nobody would come looking.” He set his glass down on the felt. “You did not tell me they were from the Red Army’s stud. You did not tell me they were in foal. You did not tell me you had a Red scout following you over the Kenkol, or that you would leave dead OGPU men in my gorge.” He looked up. “You did not tell me a great many things, Captain.”
“I told you what you needed to know.”
“No,” said the Kurbashi. “You told me what you needed me to know.” He turned his head a little, toward the ring of men. “Rahim. Ismail.”
Two men came forward out of the ring.

Strelnikov did not move. He sat quite still on the felt, with his glass in his hand, and looked at the two men, and then at the Kurbashi, and then at Bayish. His long tired face did not change at all.
“Ah,” he said, under his breath. “So that’s how it is.”

Then he threw the glass of hot tea into the Kurbashi’s face, and came up off the felt with a revolver in his hand that Bayish had not seen, and shot the man called Rahim through the body, and was gone into the dark between the tents before anyone else had moved.
After that it was very fast, and very confused, and Bayish remembered it afterwards only in pieces.

He remembered the Kurbashi on his knees by the fire with his hands over his face, and men shouting, and men running, and rifles going off into the dark at nothing. He remembered running himself, not after Strelnikov, but toward the Captain’s tent, which was the big one beside the Kurbashi’s, with a lamp burning inside it. He remembered tearing the door felt aside.

The boy was there. He was sitting on the ground at the back of the tent with a rope tied round his ankle to the tent pole, and his strapped arm against his chest, and his face white and fierce in the lamplight. When he saw Bayish he held up his good hand, and in it there was a knife, a small one, a boot knife, with which he had already cut most of the way through the rope.
“Where did you get that?”
“The Captain dropped it.” The boy’s mouth twitched. “A day ago. I sat on it.”
Bayish took the boot knife out of his hand and cut through the last strands of the rope, and pulled the boy up, and they came out of the tent together into the noise and the dark.
And then the mares began to run.

He never found out who had cut the horse lines. Strelnikov, perhaps, to cover his escape. Or one of the Kurbashi’s men, in the panic. Or no one at all, only the shooting, and the smell of blood, and the screaming of the horse that Rahim had been standing next to when he fell.
But he heard Kara-Jal.

The black stallion’s scream went up over the noise of the camp, high and terrible, the way it had gone up in the bai’s yard at Kök-Saz, and then there was a sound like the Naryn in spring flood, a great rolling thunder of hooves, and the whole herd came through the camp at a gallop in the dark. Thirty-eight mares, heavy in foal, mad with fear, with the black stallion at their head and the night full of fire and shouting, came straight through the tents and the fires and the men. Felts went down, and cooking pots, and men scattered in every direction or did not scatter fast enough, and the herd poured on through and out the far side of the camp and away up the meadow toward the hills.

Bayish had the boy by the arm. He pulled him down behind a heap of saddles and lay on top of him while the herd went by, and the ground shook under them, and a hoof went down six inches from his head.
Then it was past, and gone up the meadow into the dark, and the sound of it went away and away up the hillside toward the high ground.
Bayish got up on his knees. The camp was wreckage, fires scattered and burning in the grass, tents down, men lying where the herd had gone over them, men running. Nobody was looking at him.
“The grey,” he said. “Where’s the grey?”

She was there. She came out of the dark between the burning tents at a trot, with her head high and her wall eye rolling white in the firelight, and stopped in front of him, and stood. She had not run with the herd. She had not run at all.
He put the boy up on her back, and got up behind him, and turned her up the meadow after the herd, into the dark.
At the top of the meadow, where the ground rose toward the hills, he pulled her up for a moment and looked back.

The Kurbashi was standing by his ruined fire in the middle of the camp, with his face wet and red where the tea had scalded it, looking up the meadow after them. He did not raise a rifle. He did not call out. He only stood there, a small neat man in a silk coat in the middle of the wreckage, and looked.
Then he lifted one hand, slowly, and laid it flat on his chest, over his heart, and bowed his head.
It was the gesture a host makes to a guest who is leaving.
Zhakupov met them at the head of the meadow an hour before dawn, coming down out of the gorge on his big Don horse with the carbine across his saddle and a face like thunder.
“I heard the shooting,” he said. “You were not back.”
“It hasn’t been two dawns.”

“I can’t count,” said the sergeant. He looked at the boy sitting in front of Bayish on the grey, with his strapped arm and the boot knife still in his good hand. “So. This is the one with the strips of shirt.”
“This is the one.”

Zhakupov took the boy in, from the felt round his head to the boot knife. Then he leaned down from the saddle and held out his hand, and after a moment the boy took it, and they shook, gravely, like two men at a bazaar agreeing a price.
“The lieutenant said to tell you,” said Zhakupov, straightening, “that he has written you up for three separate offences, and will add a fourth if you get killed.”
“Tell him I’ll sign all four.”
The sergeant handed him the carbine, and unbuckled the cartridge belt from his own saddle, Bayish’s belt with the hundred and six rounds, and handed that across too.
“Where’s the Captain?”

“Gone.” Bayish buckled on the belt. His fingers knew how to do it without him. “When the herd broke, he went with it. Up there.” He pointed with his chin at the dark hills to the east, above the meadow, where the herd had gone thundering up into the night. “He’ll catch the stallion. The mares will follow the stallion. He’ll take what he can and go east, toward the high passes. Toward China.”
“On his own?”
“He’s always been on his own.”

They found the herd at first light, scattered across a long bare hillside a mile above the camp, grazing, as if nothing had happened. Mares are like that. A herd that has run itself out in the night will stop where it stops and put its head down and eat, and if you did not know, you would never think they had been mad with fear three hours before.

There were twenty-nine on the hillside. Bayish counted them twice. Three lay dead at the bottom of the meadow, where the herd had gone through the camp and they had gone down among the tents and fires and been trampled by the others. One more had fallen in a ravine in the dark and broken her back, and lay at the bottom of it, still breathing, and Zhakupov climbed down and shot her.
Thirty-five had come out of the camp. Twenty-nine were here.
“Five,” Bayish said.

He walked the edge of the hillside, bent over, reading the ground, while the sergeant and the boy sat their horses and watched. It did not take long. The ground here was bare and soft, and it was all there for anyone who could read it. The herd had come up the slope in the dark and stopped. Then a man on foot had come up after them, walking, one of the camp ponies on a rope behind him. He had gone in among the mares, unhurried, and caught the stallion, which had stood for him, and saddled it. Then he had driven five mares off the edge of the herd, the five nearest, and gone away east along the hillside toward the high ground, on the black horse, with the pony on its rope and the five mares in front.
The black stallion’s prints were big and round and deep, a heavy horse with a tall man on him, going fast.
“He’s riding Kara-Jal,” Bayish said.
“Is that bad?”

Bayish looked east, where the tracks went away along the hillside and up toward a long grey ridge, and beyond it a line of mountains with snow on them, and above the mountains a sky that had gone the colour of slate, low and heavy, with no light in it at all.
“There’s snow coming,” he said. “And he’s on a stallion that’s never been ridden in mountains, driving five mares in foal toward a pass. Yes. It’s bad.”

He sent the boy back with Zhakupov, to bring the twenty-nine down to the gorge and hold them there with the privates. The boy argued. Bayish let him argue for a while, and then said, “Your mother,” and the boy stopped arguing and looked at the ground. He had not stopped holding the knife.
“Keep it,” Bayish said. “You earned it. You sat on it a whole day.”
“Will you come back?”
Bayish looked at him.

“I said I’d bring you back to your mother,” he said. “I didn’t say anything about me.” He turned the grey’s head toward the east. “Go on. Watch the bay mare with the white blaze, the one by the rocks. She’s lame on the near fore. Don’t let them push her.”
The snow began an hour later.

It came out of the east, into his face, the way snow comes in those hills in late October: not falling but driving, flat and hard and fine as sand, on a wind that came down off the high passes and went straight through his coat. In ten minutes the hillside was white. In twenty the tracks he was following were half filled. In an hour he could see perhaps fifty yards in front of him, and then thirty, and then nothing but grey and white and the dark shape of the grey’s head with the snow caking on her mane.

But the tracks were still there. Big round deep prints in the new snow, half filled, softening, still clear enough. The stallion was heavy and the snow was not yet deep. Strelnikov was not hiding his trail any more. He had no time. He was racing the storm to the pass, as Bayish was, and he was losing, as Bayish was.

The ground went up. Rock now, under the snow. A long ridge that narrowed and narrowed, with the land falling away on the left into a white emptiness that Bayish could not see the bottom of and could hear only as a hollow roaring of wind. On the right the mountain went up, a wall of black rock with snow driving across its face.
The path between them was a ledge. A herders’ path, used for a thousand years, a yard wide in places, less in others, going along the face of the mountain above the gorge toward the pass.
The tracks went along it.

Bayish got down. He led the grey onto the ledge on foot, with the reins over his shoulder and the carbine in his right hand, close against the rock wall, and she came behind him carefully in his footprints, as she had come up the scree on the Kenkol in the dark, with her nose almost on his back.
They went along it for perhaps a quarter of an hour.

Then the ledge widened a little, into a place where the rock wall bent back and made a shelf, ten yards long and three wide, before the path narrowed again and went on round a shoulder of the mountain out of sight. And on the shelf, against the rock, standing with their tails to the wind and their heads down and the snow piling on their backs, were five mares and a camp pony.
The stallion was not there.

Bayish stopped at the edge of the shelf. The mares lifted their heads and looked at him, and one of them, a chestnut he knew, called once, low, and dropped her head again. They were finished. They could go no further, and they knew it, the way horses know, and they had stopped.
He looked at the snow on the shelf. A man’s prints, and the stallion’s, going on round the shoulder of the mountain onto the narrow path beyond. Not long ago. The edges were still sharp.
Strelnikov had left the mares. He had seen they could go no further, and he had left them on the shelf in the storm, and gone on alone on the stallion, toward the pass.
Bayish stood there a moment with the snow driving into his face. Then he went on.

The path round the shoulder of the mountain was barely a path at all. A crack along the face of the rock, two feet wide, with the wind coming round the corner like a solid thing, and the gorge on the left, invisible, roaring. He went along it with his back to the rock and the grey behind him, step by step. The grey did not hesitate once. He did not let himself think about what that meant.

Round the shoulder, the path opened out again, a little, into a slope of broken rock and snow that went up toward a notch in the ridge. The pass. It was there, just, a darker grey against the grey of the storm, two hundred yards above him.
And halfway up the slope, a black horse.

Kara-Jal had stopped. He was standing on the slope with his legs braced and his head down and his black mane streaming sideways in the wind, and he would not go on. Strelnikov was on his back, kicking him, hauling at the reins, the arm going up and down with the whip, and the stallion was not moving. He was standing quite still on the slope, a black shape against the white, and looking up at the pass.
Strelnikov turned in the saddle and saw Bayish.

He did not reach for his carbine at once. He sat there on the black horse in the driving snow and looked down the slope, and Bayish thought he could see the long tired face, the grey at the corners of the mouth. Then the Captain laughed. Bayish could not hear it, over the wind, but he saw it, the head going back.
Then he unslung his carbine.
They fired at the same moment.

Strelnikov’s shot went past Bayish’s ear with a snap like a breaking stick, and behind him the grey threw up her head. Bayish’s did not go past anything. He saw it hit. The Captain jerked in the saddle as if someone had caught him by the collar, and his carbine went out of his hands and away down the slope into the snow, and he sat back hard, with both fists dragging on the reins.
The stallion went up.

He went up on his hind legs, high, higher, with his forefeet striking at the air and his black mane flying and the weight of the man pulling his head back and back. For a moment he stood there against the white, black and enormous, upright as a man. Then his hind feet went out from under him on the broken rock and the snow, and he went over sideways off the edge of the slope, into the gorge.
He went without a sound. So did the man.
Bayish stood on the slope for a long time.

He stood until his hands were so cold he could not feel the carbine, and the snow was piling on his hat and his shoulders, and the grey had come up beside him and was standing with her head against his back. At last he went up the slope, slowly, to the place where the stallion had been.

There was nothing there. Only the big round prints of the stallion in the snow, deep and scuffed where he had reared, and then the long raw scrape of his hind feet at the edge, where the rock went down into the roar of the gorge.
And above it, between the edge and the notch of the pass, the snow. Smooth and white, driven into ridges by the wind, unmarked by anything at all.
Then he looked down at his carbine, and at the cartridge belt, and counted. He had fired once. One hundred and five.

He knew where that one had gone. He stood there in the storm and thought about a dry valley above Andijan, and a boy of seventeen who never stopped talking, and he waited to feel what he had thought for four years he would feel. Nothing came. Only the cold, and the wind, and the grey’s breath on the back of his neck.
A black horse, the old men said, belonged to somebody else.

He turned round, and went back down the slope to the grey, and took her rein. They went back along the crack in the rock, and round the shoulder of the mountain, to the shelf where five mares and a camp pony stood with their heads down in the snow, waiting for somebody to tell them what to do.
“Come on,” he said to them. “Come on, girls. We’re going home.”

They carried Lieutenant Ivanchuk down out of the gorge on a litter of two rifles and a blanket, with the two privates at the poles and Sergeant Zhakupov walking beside him, holding his hand when he thought nobody was looking.

He was fevered by then, and very pale, and talked a good deal. He talked about Poltava, and his mother’s cherry trees, and the Revolution, and how in ten years there would be electricity in every village in the Chatkal. At the mouth of the gorge, where the path went down toward the valley and Namangan and the surgeon, he made them stop, and put the litter down, and he lay looking up at Bayish, who was sitting the grey beside him with the carbine across his saddle.
“Give me that,” he said, and held out his hand.
Bayish gave him the carbine.
Ivanchuk held it on his chest for a moment, looking at it. Then he held it out again, butt first.

“It’s registered,” he said. “As of now. Weapon of the OGPU, Talas district detachment, on loan to Comrade Kenje uulu, B., for the recovery of state property.” He shut his eyes. “Sergeant, write that down.”
“Written, Comrade Lieutenant,” said Zhakupov, who was not writing anything.
“Good.” The lieutenant opened his eyes again. “I’ll put you up for a decoration. They’ll refuse it, because of the four offences. But I’ll put you up.”
Then the young man from Poltava smiled for the first time since the ford, a tired lopsided boy’s smile, and lifted his hand an inch off the blanket, and let it fall.

The privates picked up the poles. Zhakupov came over and stood at the grey’s shoulder for a moment, and put his hand flat on her neck, and then went after his lieutenant down the path toward the valley without a word.
They went home the way they had come, Bayish and the boy and thirty-four mares, north through the dry hills and up into the walnut forest. It took them nine days to reach the Chatkal.

It was slow going. The mares were tired, and heavy, and some of them lame, and they could not be pushed. Bayish did not push them. He let them graze where there was grass and drink where there was water, and in the evenings he walked among them with the boy and looked at their legs and their eyes and their bellies, and spoke to them in the morning voice, the nonsense voice, and they came to know it and to come to it. The boy learned it too. By the fourth day he could bring the herd in off a hillside on his own, one-handed, on a borrowed Kurbashi pony, calling to them low.

His arm was healing. Aimkan’s salt water and the priest’s mutton fat between them had done what they could, and the rest the boy’s own young body had done. He could move the fingers now, and on the sixth day he took the strap off and rode with the arm free and did not say anything about it, and Bayish did not either.

At the walnut-gatherers’ camp the old woman with the dried-apple face came out among the sacks to watch them pass, and nodded once, firmly, as if something had been settled, and went back to her fire.

At the hollow among the birches where the priest’s yurt had stood, there was nothing. A ring of flattened grass, and a circle of ash, and the snow melting off it. Father Mattai had gone down to his winter quarters, wherever they were, with his felts and his wooden book and his walnut pot.
Bayish sat the grey at the edge of the hollow for a while and looked at the ring in the grass.

He put his hand into his coat, to the inside pocket, where the priest’s pinch of bread was, wrapped in its scrap of white felt and tied with white thread. He had kept it there for eleven days against his chest, and it was still soft and still warm. He did not know if it was still alive. He did not know how you would tell.
He took his hand out of his coat, and rode on.
Aimkan was standing in the door of her stone house when they came up the side valley, with the ladle in her hand, as if she had been standing there for a fortnight.

She looked at her son on the Kurbashi’s pony, with his arm free and a boot knife in his belt and his face burned brown by the hills. She looked at the thirty-four mares spreading out to graze on the slope below the house, and at the man on the grey.

She did not hit him this time. She put the ladle down on the step, and went out across the yellow leaves under the poplars, and took her son down off the pony with her own hands, as if he were five years old, and held him.
Bayish sat on the grey and looked at the poplars.
That night, in the house, after the boy was asleep, he gave her two things.
The first was the strip of white felt off the grey’s brow. He untied it himself, with some trouble, because his knot was a bad one, and held it out to her across the stove.
“You said you’d take it off yourself,” he said. “If I brought him back.”
Aimkan took the felt and looked at it. She folded it, carefully, into a small square, and put it into the front of her dress.
The second was the priest’s pinch of bread.

He took it out of his coat and put it into her hand, the little warm bundle in its white felt and white thread. She knew what it was before she had untied it. He saw it in her face. She held it in her open palm and looked at it, and Bayish looked away.

“Father Mattai gave it to me,” he said. “In the hills. He said to keep it warm. He said it’s given to brides, and new priests, and to the head of a family when the herd divides.” He looked at the stove. “Your family’s herd divided, I think. In the summer of the Flight. And nobody gave you any.”
Aimkan closed her hand over the bread.
“My mother had it,” she said, very low. “Before. We had it from her mother. I lost it on the ice above the Kökjal. I put the pot down to carry his sister and I never picked it up again.”

She got up then, and went to the chest by the wall, and took out a small wooden bowl, and put the bread into it, and a little flour from a sack, and a little water from the jug, and began to work it with her fingers, slowly, in the lamplight, with her back to him.
Bayish lay down on the felt by the stove and pulled his coat over himself and watched the lamp until he slept.
They went over the Kenkol three days later, in clear weather, on new snow.

The boy came with him as far as the pass. Aimkan had said he could. She had said it at the door of the house in the morning, with her arms folded, looking at Bayish and not at her son: As far as the pass, and then he comes home. And if he goes one step past the pass, I will come over the mountain and fetch him myself, and you after him. And the boy had grinned, for the first time Bayish had ever seen, a wide sudden grin that made him look about twelve.
They brought the herd up the long south side in the morning, slowly, with the mares strung out along the trail in the snow and the sun very bright, and came to the notch at noon.
Bayish stopped the grey below it, as he had stopped there in the dark nearly three weeks before, and looked up.
The notch was white. New snow lay across it, smooth and deep and blazing in the sun, blown into long soft ridges by the wind. Nothing had crossed it since the snow came. Nothing at all.
Except, across the very top of the notch, from one side to the other, a single line of tracks.

A horse’s tracks. Unshod. A tall horse, long in the stride, light on its feet, the prints clean-edged and sharp, as if they had been made a minute ago. They came out of the unbroken snow on the eastern shoulder of the pass, where no horse could have come from, and went across the gap, and into the unbroken snow on the western shoulder, where no horse could have gone.
They did not come up from the south. They did not go down to the north. They went across.
The boy, beside him, on the Kurbashi’s pony, had gone very still.
Bayish sat and looked at the tracks for a long time. The mares came up behind him one by one and stopped, and stood, and steamed in the sun, and did not cross the tracks until he did.

Then he touched the grey with his heel, and she stepped forward, across the line, carefully, so as not to tread on any of the prints. The mares came after her, one by one, all thirty-four, and not one of them trod on them either.

At the north side of the notch the boy turned back. He did not say goodbye. He sat on his pony at the top of the pass and watched Bayish and the herd start down the long scree toward the Kenkol valley, and when Bayish looked back from the first switchback he lifted his good hand.
Bayish raised his. Then the switchback took him round, and the boy was gone.

The scree was loose under the new snow, as it had been three weeks before, and the light was beginning to go. Far below, the Kenkol ran away north in the dusk toward the Talas, and Chong-Talas, and a corral with its cut rails mended and its gate standing open. Bayish got down and took the grey’s rein, and started down ahead of her, with thirty-four mares coming after them one by one in the snow.
He went at her head, the way he always did. He did not walk behind horses.

Ormon Satarov was the name on the cover of eleven of the forty-one Ottuk Library books, more than any other writer in the series. It was not his real name. For sixty years the only facts anyone had about him were the ones he put in his books, and readers in the villages took those for granted: he had been a cavalry scout, he knew horses better than people, and he had ridden over every pass he wrote about.

All three were true. In 2020, when we went through the contracts file of Talas Kitep, the publishing house that had inherited the series, we found the payment slips for all eleven books made out to one man. He was a veterinary surgeon on a state farm in the Chatkal, born on the upper Talas around 1900. In 1919 he joined a volunteer horse unit as a boy, and he spent the early 1920s as a scout on the Turkestan Front in the Fergana. He was demobilised in 1925, the year in which The Rider from Kenkol is set, and worked with horses for the rest of his life. He began writing in his sixties, after he retired, in the winter months.

He wrote in Iradi because, as he said in a letter to his editor that survives in the file, “the horses do not understand Russian”. The Ottuk books were meant to be cheap, quick reading for the countryside: twenty-seven tyiyn, about a hundred and fifty pages, a painted cover and a chase. He gave the series what it asked for. He also gave it things it had not asked for, which the censor’s pencil found on almost every page of his typescripts: juniper smoke, the malka, priests in yurts, black bulls, and a rider on a white horse at the top of a pass who is never explained. He seems to have known which passages would be cut. Some of his typescripts carry notes in his own hand beside the censor’s, and we have printed the one from chapter Six of this book.

The Rider from Kenkol came out in 1964 as No. 7 in the series, between The Salt Road (1962) and The Last of the Ottuk (1968), the book that closed the series. It sold better than anything else he wrote, and it is the one older readers still mention first. The 1964 edition lost about a tenth of the text. This translation restores it from his typescript, which survived among the Talas Kitep papers, and marks each restored passage in a note.
His family have asked us to keep his own name off the cover, as he did. We have kept the name he chose.
Aidana Mukash kyzy
Iradi words are given in the spelling used in this translation. A few Russian and other words that the original leaves untranslated are included.
akyel: the slender golden riding horse of the Talas and the Fergana, prized by every army that came through. The Red Army bought them as remounts.
aryk: an irrigation channel.
bai: a rich man, usually a landowner or the owner of large flocks. After 1917 the word became an accusation.
bakshy: a shaman. The church has condemned them since the days of the Kokand khans.
basmachi: the armed bands who fought the Soviet power in Turkestan in the early 1920s. They were part rebels and part bandits, depending on the band and the year.
Chongtor: the short, stocky mountain horse of the herders, hard-footed and unshod.
chervontsy: gold-backed Soviet banknotes, introduced in 1922.
elechek: the white headdress, wound high, of a married woman.
ene: mother.
ırchy: a bard who sings the old songs, often on horseback.
Kapitan: Russian, “captain”.
kenje: the youngest son.
kun: restitution, the price paid under custom law for a death or injury. Toguz, “ninefold”, is the heaviest fine.
kurbashi: the commander of a basmachi band.
kyzy, uulu: “daughter of”, “son of”. They follow the father’s name: Nurdin Tölögön uulu is Nurdin, son of Tölögön.
malka: the holy leaven of the mountain churches, the “mother leaven”, said to descend from the bread of St. Janyl. It is kept in a wooden pot, renewed each Holy Thursday, and given, never sold.
Morkhan: the old bull-headed god of darkness, whom the church identifies with Satan. Black is his colour.
OGPU: the Soviet political police of the 1920s.
omin: amen.
soviet: a council. A village soviet was the local government.
White Rider: the rider on a white horse who, in Iradi belief, comes down off the mountain for a soul and carries it home over the pass.

In the night, ten riders cut the rails of the state stud at Chong-Talas and drive off forty-one golden mares in foal and the black stallion Kara-Jal. The militia’s one lorry is away in Kara-Buura. So Bayish Kenje uulu, Red cavalry scout turned horse-breaker, saddles his wall-eyed grey mare and goes after them alone, over the Kenkol Pass, with a hundred and twenty rounds. Ahead of him rides a man he has followed once before, and a debt that goes back four years to a dry valley above Andijan. And at the top of the pass, above them all, a rider on a white horse is watching. First published in Iradi in 1964 and cut by the censor, The Rider from Kenkol is the best-loved of the Ottuk Library westerns. This first English translation restores the passages that were cut.
